en: The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Reality.
[Expression of Benediction: Homage to the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī!
Risen from the circle of the soles of her feet, fanned by the wind, radiant with flashes of lightning,
having burnt the three enemies, honored by the three worlds, and drenched in streams of nectar— she [is victorious].

May Vārāhikā protect you—she who is permeated by the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom, free from turbidity, bestowing a mass of bliss, and devoid of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence. ||1||
The *Marmakalikā-pañjikā*.
Oṃ, homage to the illustrious Vajravilāsinī!
By the playful movement of the *caṇḍālī*, he who has caused the universe to arise from his own station—
Creating abundant great bliss in all directions, absorbed in the arising of his own awakening,
he has attained the state of nirvāṇa even while seated upon the tip of a lotus.
We bow to that [Goddess] by whom even two simultaneous risings are instantly assumed for the sake of innate bliss.
May this Lord, whose splendor is ever-new like the ocean and who has attained union with the mere expanse of the sky, protect the world;
for upon his body, the twilight—possessing lightning and sporting with the thunderbolt—shines forth.
I am the disciple of all those who know the divine methods,
who abide in the profound bliss of the deep meaning of the Vajra Goddess.
This should be forgiven here, that this friend has composed this manual;
for in the darkness, it is the friend alone who illuminates all things.
If it is argued that "this ultimate truth is profound and commentators are not of such a caliber," then let it be so; however, [let us proceed] here with respect to the conventional portion.
And also reverence.

When the Blessed One Saṃvarārṇava had vanished, the Master Samādhivajra, having received grace from Vajravilāsinī and drawn forth the oral instructions from the lotus feet of his true guru, composed a sādhana of the illustrious Vajravārāhī— who is of the nature of the two Cāṇḍālīs consisting of cause and fruit, and who is of the nature of the Innate (*sahaja*)— which is delightful, adorned with a multitude of most excellent qualities. Therefore, even by means of the first two verses, she whose essential nature is characterized by ten distinct attributes in each verse, mutually interconnected, [is revealed].

I invoke Vajravārāhī— who is of that very nature, who instantly dispels the darkness of worldly ignorance, who generates a mass of bliss characterized by the fourth moment brought about by the cessation [of suffering], and who is the counterpart to the protection of her own offspring— by means of a benediction,
beginning with the words "Risen," and so forth.
The connection is: "May Vārāhikā protect you. *Vara* is the bodhicitta, so called because it chooses (*varayati*) or desires the welfare of all beings;
or rather, *vara* itself is *vāraḥ*. [The root] *vara-*...
In the sense of "desire to obtain," it belongs to the *curādi* group and ends in a long vowel; the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*.
Alternatively, the substitution of *ā* for *a* occurs because the word belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

Or else, it is called *vāra* because it covers (*āvṛṇoti*) the body at every pore; thus *vāra* refers to semen (*śukra*), derived from the root *vṛṇ* in the sense of covering, belonging to the *pṛṣādi* group.

She is called Vārāhikā because she draws forth—that is, follows—Heruka, who resides in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) in the form of a drop (*bindu*), from the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*).
The suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of a name.

Alternatively, she is called Vārāhī by etymological derivation (*nirukti*): she has struck with her trunk (*kara*) her husband, the Lord (*vara*), who is situated in the wheel of bliss, just as a proud woman might strike him; thus, from the root *vṛ* (to choose) ending in the suffix *aṇ* with the addition of the feminine suffix *ḍāp*, she is Vārāhī.
The sequence of instruction here is also written down:
the word *vā* denotes air (*vāyu*) in this context, as the verbal root *vā-* has the meaning of "going."
For it is by his very impulsion that this goddess arises.
And thus it has been revealed in the *Sādhana* by Śabara-pāda: "Having contracted the mouth of the Rākṣasa and having kindled her radiant splendor,
she is Vārāhī, stationed upon the wheel of the palm of the hand."
It is thus designated.
Then, from the letter *ra*, there arises a line in the form of fire;
it is the letter *a* or *avadhūtī*, for she is indeed the bliss of all phenomena.
The letter *ra* is a line composed of fire; when it moves by means of its own nature (*ātman*),
the letter *a*, whose form is radiant bliss, is to be perceived here as well.
Or, through the conjunction of two, it may be of medium length;
the letter *ha*, situated in the wheel of bliss (*sukhacakra*), is embraced by that line.
Then, flooding the Goddess, the letter *i* is called the *bindu*;
from that arises a certain supramundane [wisdom] which bestows supramundane bliss.

This Lakṣmī, whose wealth is inexhaustible, is this very goddess in the form of the syllable *Ī*. One should [worship] this seven-syllabled goddess through the purification of knowledge of the three worlds.
The hero Heruka spoke this Herukī to Vārāhī:
"Indeed, the entire universe, though false and characterized by violent attachment, is manifested through her."
For this very reason, the Blessed One spoke even of Caṇḍālī Herukī.
For this very reason, in the first verse of the *Mūlatantra*:
"Now, therefore, I shall speak of the secret," in this [verse]...

Our venerable teacher has explained the Caṇḍālī-yoga as follows: "From the syllable *A*, which is the nature of Vajravārāhī residing in the nirmāṇacakra, through the contact of the syllable *Ha*— which is the nature of Saṃvara residing in the sukha-cakra— with the flame in the form of the sun represented by the letter *Ra*, there occurs the vibration of the *bindu*."
This, however, having been received from Nandipāda through oral tradition (from ear to ear) by the venerable Sadguru Dāsapāda, has been made public.
Therefore, because it is a great traditional teaching, the virtuous should also pay close attention to it.
He asks, "Of what nature is she? and says:
"Gone upward," and so forth. "Gone upward" means she has ascended.
Regarding "from the *talacakra*": because it is situated at the base (*tala*) of the *dharmacakra*, the *saṃbhogacakra*, and the *mahāsukhacakra*, the *talacakra* is the *nirmāṇacakra*.
The phrase "shaken by the wind" (aniladhūtā) means impelled by the apāna-vāyu.

"Resplendent like a flash of lightning" (vidyucchaṭābhāsvareti) means shining intensely like a streak of lightning, because she consists of the fire of knowledge (jñānāgni), being composed of light or possessing passion (sarāga).
For this very reason, this Blessed Lady is the burner of the wood that is the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*).
And it has been shown in the *Vasantatilaka-ṭīkā*:
"Her brilliance exceeds the fierce mass of lightning flashing from within the layers of dark clouds."
I bow to you, Herukī, Mother of the World, who simultaneously incinerates both the sentient beings and their environment.

I bow to you, who possess the brilliance of the submarine fire, born from the union of the vajra and the lotus within the ocean-like cavity of the navel-cakra, and who are ever-eager to drink the essence of the finest nectar.
Regarding the phrase "dagdhāritritaya" (the three enemies burnt): by the word *ara*, the spokes (*ārā*) are meant; that which possesses these is the *ari*, namely the wheel (*cakra*).
She by whom the three wheels—known as the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Mahāsukha—are burnt, rendered devoid of intrinsic nature, and made of one flavor; she is thus [described].
"Worshipped by the three worlds" means she is honored by the three worlds: heaven, the mortal realm, and the netherworld (pātāla).
Or [it is so called] because of the accomplishment of oneself in that form through body, speech, and mind; thus,
"bathed in a stream of nectar."

It is flooded— that is, nourished— by streams of nectar flowing from the moon (the *sudhādīdhiti*), which emerges immediately after the torment of the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*) situated in the wheel of bliss (*sukhacakra*);

and it has become established, as it were, because it has attained a state of total integration with uninterrupted innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) through the complete uprooting of the entire collection of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, at that very moment, that same Blessed Lady consisting of gnosis (*jñānamayī*), free from the turbidity of the knower and the known, must be brought forth by the practitioners of yoga in an inconceivable form.
This very point is clarified by the phrase "smeared with the essence of the Buddha-gnosis" (*buddhajñānarasāvile*).

Here, "Buddha" refers to Akṣobhya—the Supreme Lord who is the *bindu*, whose root, middle, and tip are attained through the union of the assembly of the Vajra and the Lotus, and who resides in the region prior to the state of cessation (*virama*).
Therefore, that knowledge which has arisen is like the sexual pleasure experienced for the first time by a young maiden,
like the tasting of a particular extraordinary flavor,
or like a distinguished dream seen by a mute.

The reality of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is unmanifest; its "tasting" (*rasāsvādana*) is that by which [the mind] becomes undisturbed, meaning it is exclusively intent upon that alone and remains so until the [final] occasion.
For this very reason, it is free from turbidity.

"Defiled" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth; it is "free from" or devoid of them, because even these are included within great bliss (*mahāsukha*) itself. And it has been said:
"Wherever the mind goes, one should apply the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) there."
Having moved, where will you go? For everything is indeed composed of that.
And so it is said:
"By whatever state of being the minds of men are joined,
they attain the nature of that very thing, just as a crystal assumes the form of everything before it."
Alternatively, what pleasure is there? That from which anger arises is *kaluṣa* (turbid); *virāga* [is derived as follows]:
*kapilā* (an ant), with the substitution of *l* for *r* due to grammatical rules (*ditva*) or etymological derivation (*nirukta*).
She is devoid of that; "turbid" means sin, for there is an absence of sin characterized by detachment,
since even sin is nothing but detachment itself.
And so the venerable Āryadeva said:
"There is no sin greater than dispassion (virāga), nor is there merit greater than happiness.
[Yet] falling away (cyuti) arises from dispassion, and from dispassion the arising of suffering occurs.
From suffering comes the exhaustion of the elements for men; from that exhaustion, death arises. Thus it is said.

Regarding the term *sānandasandohada*: bliss (*ānanda*) refers to those [states] ending with the *virama*; that in which there is the complete milking (*sandoha*), that is, the drawing forth and rendering free of appearance (*nirābhāsīkaraṇa*) of all things together with those very [blisses], is the "mass of bliss" (*ānandasandoha*); it is so called because it bestows (*dadāti*) that.

Alternatively, it is called *sandoha* because by means of it the sense organs, their objects, and the consciousnesses are correctly perceived (*samyagdṛśyante*) and rendered free from appearance (*nirābhāsīkriyante*). It is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Furthermore, it is the *sānandasandoha*, meaning that this *sandoha* is accompanied by the joys ending with *viramānanda*, having attained a state of single flavor (*ekarasa*);
it is so called because it bestows that.
Alternatively, the word "she" (*sā*) is an epithet of Vārāhikā;

it means she is the bestower of a mass of bliss (*ānanda-sandoha*), whether that be worldly prosperity consisting of the enjoyment of garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth, or that which is supramundane. Let alone the worldly [attainment] for those who worship this Blessed Lady—
The meaning is that even supramundane bliss is an *abhyudaya* (prosperity).
And it has been stated in this very *sādhana*: "But this one bestows the means for happiness."

In the reading *svānandasandohada*, [the term] refers to that which bestows a beautiful mass (*sandoha*)— that is, a collection— of blisses, due to the intense awakening of the four blisses characterized by the four moments (*kṣaṇa*), namely the variegated (*vicitra*) and so forth, which are situated at the root-jewel, the middle-jewel, and the tip-jewel of the double-jeweled [cakra]. By this very statement, it is said that through the grace of this very Blessed Lady alone, the moment of meditation characterized as being difficult to attain arises.

Otherwise, how could it be that the drop (bindu), situated below the surface of one who is well-established, bestows its own mass of bliss—like the filaments of a lotus—except upon the lotus-filament itself?

"Devoid of the investigation of existence and non-existence" means: existence and non-existence refer to the eternal and the annihilated, or the aspects of the conventional and the absolute; the investigation of these is the determination of their essential nature, and she is devoid of, or separated from, such [investigation].

At that very moment, upon attaining a state of single flavor (*ekarasa*), a form inseparable from emptiness and compassion (*śūnyatā-karuṇā*) arises as the cause; for it is like a perfected mantra, equalizing the eternalist and nihilist views, which are like a husband and wife who are both demons (*piśāca*).
When, through this investigation, one has offered the funeral libation to those [extremes], one experiences only the bliss of the yoginī as the remainder.

There is also another explanation: with reference to the yoga of the *utpannakrama* (generation stage), he speaks of the Goddess who possesses a physical form and yet is of the nature of the innate (*sahaja*). "She who has arisen," and so forth. The connection is: "May that Vārāhikā protect [us]. She is called *Vārāhī* because she has struck down (*āhatavatī*) the *vāra*, which is the two-fold obscuration consisting of the nature of afflictions and the knowable (*kleśajñeya*). She covers (*āvṛṇoti*) the universe; thus she is *vāra*. She is *vārāhī* because she has destroyed that.
Even in this view, the word *Vārāhī* is established for the purpose of instruction:
the syllable *vā* signifies the meaning of that which transcends speech; the letter *ra* signifies the unification of all flavors (*rasa*); and [the vowel *ā*] signifies eternal self-experience.
The letter *kā* and the letter *ha* are the unstruck bliss (*anāhata-sukha*).
Because life has wisdom as its intrinsic nature, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indicated by that;
thus, this condensed meaning is called the *Vārāhī-tattva*.
And it has been stated by the accomplished master Kṛṣṇapāda in the *Saṃvara-nāma*:
"The word 'vā' is beyond the path of speech and is devoid of the forms of the letters 'rā' and 'ā';
it is proclaimed as the sound of Vārāhī, being the letter 'hī' which lacks a perceived cause."
Regarding the phrase "the wheel of the base has been raised," the word *tala* is also employed in the sense of that which has the nature of being below.
The "ground" (tala) is the essential nature, which is luminosity— that is to say, emptiness; that itself is the "wheel" (cakra),
because it cuts through all conceptual constructions.
Therefore, the meaning is that she arises from the power of her very vow (*praṇidhāna*), just as a wave arises from the ocean as something non-different from it.
Alternatively, the letter *a* here should be understood as being joined (*praśleṣa*) to indicate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, it should be understood that here [the phrase] "from the wheel of that" refers to this.
Regarding the term "shaken by the wind":
by the word "wind," consciousness mounted upon the wind is designated through its association with it.

Just as in the expression "the beds are crying," it is actually the persons situated on the beds who are being denoted, so too, by this consciousness—which is carried by the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*)—it is shaken, pressed, and dances in a form free from attachment; this is the meaning.
If this consciousness, accompanied by the wind, were to become dissolved, it would not fashion even the universe.
Therefore, one must exert effort in this regard.

For this very purpose, this Goddess, who is innate in nature, devoid of letters, symbols, and the like, and transcending the entire domain of speech, appears within oneself—like a rainbow, like a city of Gandharvas, or like a wondrous painting in the sky—as a collection of five rays of light emerging from five colors and five jewels;

she is manifested through the power of the jewel of the mind of aspiration for the state consisting of the five Tathāgatas, which is equal to the Bandhūka flower, amidst a diverse assembly of Yogins and Yoginīs characterized by white skulls, yellow corpses, black Kṛttis, green single banners, and so forth.
The Blessed Lady fashioned [the mandala] within the region of the stainless inner sky;
for this very reason, the Goddess, whose form is the letter *Ā*,
having attained a state of aesthetic unity (*samarasatā*) with the wind in the form of the letter *U* which is Amoghasiddhi, fashioned the *Nirmāṇacakra* in the form of the letter *Vaṃ*.
For one whose mind lacks the opportunity to be directed toward this [reality], the attainment of the uncontrived state occurs through the cessation of both winds.
And it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"O Vajragarbha of great compassion, beings are liberated by means of [this] very state."
"Beings are bound by attachment to existence and are liberated through the thorough knowledge of it.
And likewise:
"Attachment itself is the supreme friend; attachment itself is the supreme enemy."
The pure shall become like nectar, while the impure shall be worse than poison.
"Flashing with streaks of lightning" means blazing intensely with a mass of rays that remove all suffering.
"Having burnt the three enemies" [is the meaning].
She by whom the triad of enemies—the nature of the senses, their objects, and consciousness—has been rendered unperceivable as if burnt;
or else, she by whom delusion, attachment, and aversion have been burnt away, reduced to ashes.
She is "venerated by the three worlds."
The three worlds are body, speech, and mind, because they are established within oneself in their respective forms. "Venerated" means honored;
the sense is that the very act of establishing oneself in the form of the Goddess is itself the worship of the Goddess.
Regarding the phrase "bathed in a stream of nectar" (*pīyūṣadhārāplutā*):
"nectar-like" (*pīyūṣam iva pīyūṣam*) refers to happiness; thus, it means "bathed in a stream of incomparable bliss."
"Imbued with the essence of the Buddha-gnosis. Here, "Buddha" refers to the awakening to reality as it truly is.
Thus, in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"I am a Buddha because of the awakening to reality"—
that very knowledge is the *tattva* (the truth), and the *rasa* (flavor) therein is the savoring; by means of that effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*)—
"Vilā" means "joined.
Regarding "vikaluṣā":
*kaluṣa* refers to afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, or passion (*rāga*) and other such conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Devoid of that;
"by means of the mass of bliss" means she who completely purifies the mass of bliss.
Regarding the purification of the *daīpa* (the lamp),
because the three joys (*ānanda*) are not perceived as having that [lamp's] form,
or because they are included within the *sahaja* (the innate).

In the interpretation that it "arises from the mass of one's own bliss" (*svānandasandoha*), "one's own" (*sva*) refers either to the self (*ātman*) or to the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); "bliss" (*ānanda*) is the attachment directed toward that [self]; its "mass" (*sandoha*) is an uninterrupted activity.
She is the shatterer of that [duality].
The root *khaṇḍ* means "to break.
Therefore, she is devoid of any investigation into existence and non-existence.
Existence is the perception of the three;
non-existence is annihilation;
the investigation of these two is the apprehending mind, and [reality] is devoid of that.
And it was said by the Bhagavatī: "That mind which is mindless exists.
She is situated within the solar mandala of the emanation and so forth, and is enveloped by the colors beginning with *ka* and so on.
Blazing with the brilliance of a kindled fire,
resembling a thread of fine lotus fiber,
this Vidyā— which pierces the three wheels— burns away the assembly of Buddhas along with the sacrificial oblation of nectar.
May Vārāhikā, full of bliss and moving gracefully upward, manifest within your hearts. ||2||
To explain a specific meaning, he states another verse beginning with "nirmāṇa" and so forth:
"O yours," [referring to] Vārāhikā, whose connection [to the lineage] was established as before;
may she "quiver," that is, manifest.
What kind [of state] is it? He says: "situated in the solar mandala of the emanation-enemy.
First, she was situated within the solar mandala located in the emanation-wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*);
then, she arose from that wheel.
The meaning is: "due to the sovereign power of the mature mind of the practitioner.
Regarding the phrase "encircled by the letters beginning with Ka," *kādi* refers to that which has the letter *ka* as its first; thus, it is *kāli*.
That which has *a* as its first letter is *ādirāliḥ*.
By the rule "a with a becomes long," [the form is established].

Since the letter *kṣa* is produced from the letters *ka* and *ṣa*, one should exclude *kṣa*; thus, there are forty-nine letters, which are to be understood as representing the wind (*pavana*), because the wind has forty-nine [aspects].
Therefore, by the term *ālikāli*, only the two arms (the two winds) on the left and right are to be understood.
By this, the following is stated: first, she is enveloped and enclosed by the two winds.
Due to the relinquishing of both those arms,
and consequently from that very entry into the middle channel, it is subsequently "stirred by the wind," meaning impelled by the apāna wind.

Conventionally, however, it should be understood that the solar mandala itself is enveloped by the two rows of vowels and consonants joined together, winding from left to right, with their heads pointing upward.
"Blazing with intensely radiant fire" means that previously, in the *nirmāṇacakra*, that very Blessed Lady in the form of the syllable *Vaṃ* was as brilliantly resplendent as a mass of blazing fire.
The meaning is that, thereafter, it became like a flash of lightning, possessing the brilliance of a streak of lightning.
Regarding "Amṛtasavā": she is so called because her *sava*—that is, her production, birth, or origin—is from *amṛta*, the nectar.
The intended meaning is that this is due to her sovereignty over the Blessed Lady who resides in the wheel of bliss (*sukhacakra*).
Therefore, she is one by whom the three enemies are burnt, by whom the three wheels are crushed,
and who resembles a subtle lotus fiber.
That lotus-fiber and lotus-stalk fiber are both subtle and extremely subtle; thus, "subtle lotus-fiber" refers to that which has that very thing as its simile—that is, its similarity.
This is because [the avadhūtī] has non-apprehension as its intrinsic nature and because it is the very essence of the avadhūtī.
For this very reason, she is honored by the three worlds; for "maha" means worship.
The worship of the Goddess is precisely the realization of body, speech, and mind as the form of the Goddess within oneself—transcending all conceptual constructions and exceedingly subtle.
The intention is that it is logical for this very [state] to be included within that which remains as mere sound (*nāda*).
Regarding "knowledge" (*vidyā*): she who is the Goddess, whose nature is knowledge (*vid*), is the embodiment of wisdom.
She knows, thus she is "vit" (the knower). From the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing," with the suffix *kvip*.
For this very reason, that Goddess—who is flooded by a stream of nectar and whose form is the light of knowledge—is indeed bathed in ambrosia and is therefore pure (*śuddhā*).
Alternatively, "pīyūṣa" means like nectar; the meaning is that she consists of that great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Regarding the phrase "she burns the cluster of Buddhas" (*buddhakadambakaṃ dahati*): the "cluster of Buddhas" refers to the five Tathāgatas; she burns—that is, renders devoid of intrinsic nature—the individual cognition of their respective selves.
This is because the very nature of perception consists of the five Buddhas themselves.
And it was said by the Blessed One in the *Śrīguhyendra*: "This entire world has the five Buddhas as its essence."
Also in the *Saṃdhyāvyākaraṇa*:
"The aggregates themselves are indeed the Fully Awakened Ones.
The meaning is that through the perception of these, there is the perception of the entire universe itself.
Because there is no difference between the Blessed One (Bhagavān) and the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī), the goddesses are also included; or rather, they are included by the word "Buddha" itself,
according to the principle that "there is no sentient being who is not a Buddha."
Because of this statement.
For this very reason, she is "composed of awakening" (*bodhamayī*), being permeated by the essence of the Buddha’s gnosis (*jñāna*).
Regarding the reading of the compound as *vidyābuddhakadambakaṃ dahati*: "Vidyās" refers to Locanā and the others, because they go to or attain (*yanti*) "vita," which is gnosis (*jñāna*).
In that view, the term "subtle" (*sūkṣmā*) should be construed as a separate compound meaning "that which demonstrates the knowledge of non-perception.
[The phrase] "piercing through the three wheels" (*cakratrayodbhedinī*) [is explained as follows].
She whose nature it is to pierce through the three wheels (cakras) is thus described.

The sense is that she proceeds after having taken up the Lord—even though He is situated on a mountain peak—and the Goddess even though She has fallen into the interior of a lotus, and having pierced through the three wheels;
for this very reason, she is "unstained" (vikaluṣā), meaning free from affliction (kleśa).
Because it is conjoined with great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Thus it is said: "accompanied by joy" (*sānanda*); joy is the drop (*bindu*). It is that...
The attainment of the bliss of the Residue (śeṣānanda) is joined with that [bliss] as cause and effect; or rather, because of the non-difference between cause and effect, it is bliss itself.
Therefore, being honored by that, she bestows a mass of her own bliss—that is, she is the giver of a multitude of beautiful joys.
For it is only one who is himself capable that can appropriately bestow grace upon others.
Regarding the term *lalitordhvaga*: "gracefully" (*lalitena*) refers to the continuous flow of great passion (*mahārāga*) and the entry into the central channel (*madhyamā*).
The meaning is "one who goes upwards.
Alternatively, she is Lalitā, who is both bound by the great passion of non-duality (*advayamahārāga*) and one who goes upwards;
or rather, she is one who dwells in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
For this very reason, it is devoid of investigation into existence and non-existence, because investigation is impossible for that whose essential nature is bound up with great passion (*mahārāga*);
even investigation is a form of distraction (*vikṣepa*).
And that it should be "bound by great passion" is a contradiction.
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"In the ocean of awakening, where nothing is perceived, what is this bubble of an eon?"
There is also another explanation: "nirmāṇāri" and so forth. *Nirmāṇa* means arising; its *ari* (enemy) is the pure selflessness (*viśuddhanairātmya*) manifested in the form of a corpse (*śava*).

In that [corpse], one has gone to the solar disc—the mandala of the light of gnosis (*jñānālokamaṇḍala*). Here, the root *gam* (to go) has the sense of knowing (*jñāna*). Thus, it means one who has realized it.
This is because of the logical principle that all roots meaning "to go" (gati) have the sense of "to know" (jñāna).
"Enveloped by the letters beginning with Ka and so forth" means consisting of the vowels and consonants (āli-kāli).

Because this [Vidyā], whose form is wisdom (*prajñā*), has the nature of the entirety of speech; or else, "ka" and "a" are the first of those [letters] which begin with them— namely the consonants (*kādayaḥ*)—
and their initial letter is...
"Kāra" means that which is covered or enveloped by that form; alternatively, "kādayaḥ" refers to the seven groups beginning with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*.
The first of these is the letter *a*, whose nature consists of the sixteen digits (*ṣoḍaśakalā*).
She is concealed by that form,
because the letter *A* itself has the nature of concealing all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). And in the *Śrīhevajra*:
"The Yoginī’s body, situated within the midst [of the body], abides as the enclosure (saṃvara) of the letter A;
as it is externally, so it is internally— thus has that enclosure been revealed."

For even in the *Ekākṣarī Prajñāpāramitā*, she is taught as having this very nature of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*. "Blazing with a radiant fire" means that her body is resplendent with a mass of rays of light spreading throughout the universe.
Regarding "Amṛtasavā": *amṛta* is liberation (*mokṣa*); she is so called because her *sava*—her flow or emanation—is that very liberation.
Regarding "resembling a subtle lotus fiber": [she is like it in her subtlety].
Because its form originates from the exceedingly subtle lotus;
"Vidyā" means she whose nature is innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*).
Alternatively, the Goddess is she who consists of non-artificial knowledge (*akṛtrimajñāna*);

she is she who "burns the cluster of Buddhas" (*buddhakadambaka*). Here, "Buddhas" refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; their "cluster" (*kadambaka*) is their "wretched eye" (*kutsitam ambakaṃ*), which is their wrong view (*kudṛṣṭi*)—the conviction that "I alone shall subdue [myself]" and so forth.
The meaning is that it burns because it consists of destruction; for that [destruction] has as its ultimate goal the welfare of sentient beings.
And thus, regarding the Vaibhāṣika’s entry into the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, there is also a word of the Blessed One:
"I would rather become a jackal in the delightful Jetavana than that Gautama should attain the liberation of the Vaibhāṣikas. Thus [he spoke].
Alternatively, it means that she burns the clusters of Buddhas—the objects and the subjects—by enjoining them to non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Regarding the phrase "piercing the three wheels" (*cakratrayodbhedinī*):
the three wheels consist of the essential nature of body, speech, and mind.

Because it would follow that those very [elements], when fragmented, would result in the destruction of the distinguished vision; she whose nature is to break—that is, to split—that [vision] is thus described. "With bliss" (sānandā) means having the nature of innate bliss (sahajānanda).

Regarding the term *lalitordhvagā*: by means of *lalita*, which is the Great Passion (*mahārāga*), she goes—that is, she attains—the upward, transcendent object that lies beyond the sphere of speech. ||2||
Having prostrated with my head before Vajravārāhī, the Vajrayoginī who is preceded by the Vajra,
I shall explain for my own recollection the perfect accomplishment of the knowledge of reality. (3)
Establishing the subject matter by way of a salutation, he says: "Having prostrated," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "I shall speak, having attained the perfect accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*) of the knowledge of reality.
This is because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause.

Reality (*tattva*) is that which transcends the conceptual constructions of self and other, having the nature of an inexpressible, true bliss; likewise, the knowledge of that—self-cognition—is the "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*).
Thus it is said in the venerable *Hevajra*: "And reality is by way of true bliss."
Having done what? He says: "having prostrated to Vārāhī.
This means having paid homage to her who possesses the form of both Caṇḍālīs and the form of Sahaja.
[The term] "preceded by Vajra" [is used].
She who has the *vajra* as her very beginning is Vajravārāhī; the meaning is that she whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indivisible gnosis (*abhedyajñāna*).
Regarding "Vajrayoginī": she is so called because she possesses (*yoga*)—that is, is united with (*saṃyoga*)—the *vajra*, which is either the *bindu* or great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"From the head" means by means of the crown of the head.
"For one's own recollections" means for the purpose of remembering oneself.
The avoidance of restlessness is the meaning of this statement. ||3||
[Thus ends the expression of benediction.
[Now follows the procedure for external worship: a secluded mind.
Having entered a favorable place with the Lord’s image upon his lap, the wise practitioner should sit on a soft seat there and contemplate purification. (1)
He states the locus of cultivation, beginning with "solitary" and so forth.
The connection is that one should contemplate purity, complete purification, and emptiness;
for it is precisely through that cultivation that ordinary ego-conceit is dispelled.
Alternatively, for those of superior capacity, emptiness itself is the supreme protection; therefore, emptiness alone should be cultivated first. As it has been said:
"Suchness itself is the supreme protection from obstacles created by the mind;
for the purity of all phenomena everywhere is indeed suchness."
Having done what? He says: having entered a secluded place, devoid of people. "Favorable to the mind" means that which generates clarity of mind.
"Therein" means in that solitary place. "Having sat upon a seat" means having taken recourse to a seat.
"Tender" means pleasant to the touch. "Resting on the lap of the Lord" means—
The Lord is the venerable Guru; he whose crest (*kaṃ*)—his head—is marked by his insignia (*tadaṅka*) is "marked by the Lord's insignia" (*nāthāṅkaka*).
The wise one is one whose mind is free from parts (*niṣkala*), [or] pure.
[She is] the Yoginī, by me.

This venerable goddess is censured here, and although it has been established by the Guru that only those of great stature have the authority [to practice] this, it is nevertheless written down as a specific distinction.
The connection is as follows: "the wise one" (*sudhīḥ*) should "contemplate" (*vibhāvayet*), that is, produce, the "purity" (*śuddhim*) of the mind, which is its stainlessness (*nairmalyam*).
One who possesses "excellent wisdom" (*sudhīḥ*)—whether external discernment or internal spiritual discernment—is "wise" (*saprajña*); this is the meaning.
"That very Blessed Lady Prajñā is designated as Dhīti by the Buddhas," according to the words of the *Hevajra*.
To the question "Staying where?", it says: "having sat upon the seat."
It is called the *āsana* (seat) because one sits (*āsyate*) upon it, whether by means of the *vajra* or the *utsarga-maṇḍala*; this seat is the *dharmodayā*.
As it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*: "That which is divine in the form of the letter *E*, adorned in its center with the syllable *vaṃ*."
"It is the abode of all happiness, a jewel-casket for the Buddha.
Relying upon that,
it is called "delicate."
"Captivating" means not loose, that is to say, pleasant to the touch.
"Therein" refers to the *dharmodayā*.
To the question of how its purification is to be cultivated, he says: "having entered the place, one remains."

"Ripened by all phenomena" means that one takes as an object the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Regarding "solitary": *jana* refers to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it is always born.
It is devoid of that.
And it is said in the Vajraḍāka: "In a solitary place, and in those states free from conceptual constructions such as the internal sentient being and so forth."
Alternatively, it is "solitary" because it arises from maidens born of the Vajra family and so forth.
As it is said in that very same [text]: "It is solitary because it arises from maidens born of a distinguished lineage such as the Vajra family, which is praised by all the Tathāgatas.
For this very reason, it is "conducive to the mind."

The sense is that for one whose mind is stained by the impurity of conceptual constructions such as "this has been done" and "this has not been done," everything in the universe is adverse because of the constant occurrence of suffering; whereas for one with a non-conceptual mind, there is a constant occurrence of happiness. For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One: [The passage continues: "...for one who is free from conceptual construction, there is always the presence of bliss."* *(Note: The Sanskrit fragment provided in the source text appears to be part of a longer citation, likely from a Buddhist treatise on meditation or Abhidharma.)*
"The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated, and being concentrated, one understands things as they truly are.
To the question "Being of what nature?", he says: "He whose crest-jewel is marked by the Lord" (*nāthāṅkaka*).
The Lord (*nātha*) is the *bindu*; that which is marked by it (*tadaṅka*) is its sign; and *ka* is bliss. He who possesses that [bliss] as his crest-jewel is *nāthāṅkaka*.
Because bliss devoid of the drop (bindu) is of the nature of suffering;

or else, "Nātha" refers to the Guru, and "aṅka" means a mark or sign; "ka" means bliss, where that [bliss] exists, for that bliss was imparted by the Guru during the consecrations of Wisdom and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that by generating great passion from the very sound of "vajra" and "padma," purification must be performed within the union of emptiness and compassion.
And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"In the supreme rite, there is neither the object of meditation nor the meditator."
There is neither body, nor object of grasping, nor grasper; there is no flesh, no blood, no excrement,
no urine, no loathing, no delusion, and no purity or holiness.
It is also stated in the *Vajradharma-sādhana*:
"One should cause the throbbing secret vajra to enter the lotus."
There, having stabilized the mind, one should cultivate non-conceptual great bliss.
One should recite: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness."
Therefore, in this system of Great Passion (mahārāga), the tradition (āmnāya) is that emptiness (śūnyatā) itself must be meditated upon as the reality. ||1||
Thereafter, having written the heart-mantra of Vajradhara with the sixth Conqueror (the letter *va*) recited three times, one should honor it with red flowers using the ring finger. ||2||
He states another injunction: "Thereafter," and so forth.
The connection is that immediately after that, one should make the heart of the Vajra-holder (vajradhara) worshipped with red flowers.
Because it is indivisible, the *vajra* is innate bliss (*sahajasukha*); that which holds this is the *vajradhara*, namely the *bindu*.
This is because the *bindu* is perceived only when it is conjoined with bliss.
And it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"The Blessed One takes the form of semen; that bliss is known as the *kāminī*."
One should worship that *dharmodayā* of the Vajradhara with red flowers—such as the unfading *karavīra*, *bandhūka*, and so forth—because it is his singular focal point (*ekaniṣṭhatva*).
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of indicating another matter to be expressed:

having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) according to the intention set forth in the two verses to be recited hereafter, one should subsequently worship the *dharmodayā*. This is the meaning.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this rule follows immediately after the instruction itself;
in that view, the particle *ca* has the sense of "also" (*api*).
Having done what? He says: "having well-drawn" (*saṃllikhya*). The meaning is: having drawn it clearly with a span of three finger-breadths (*tryaṅgula*).
By whom? He says: "by the sixth Jina."
By Akṣobhya. Because Akṣobhya is liquid and black, the meaning is "by means of black-colored *madana*.
This is because in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*, Akṣobhya is established as the sixth Tathāgata.
And likewise, in the *Lūyipādīyābhisamaya*, it is said:
"In the aggregate of consciousness is Vajrasattva; in the state of all Tathāgatas is Śrī Herukavajra.
[This is] "recited with the three syllables."
Having purified [the ink] three times with "oṃ āḥ hūṃ," he asks with what it should be written: "with the ring finger," that is,
with the ring finger of the left hand.
Because the observances (*saṃvara*) consist of left-handed conduct (*vāmācāra*).
Thus it is said in the *Śrīsaṃvara*:
"The yogi should always practice left-handed conduct; he should step forward with the left foot."
There is also another explanation: the heart of Vajradhara is the *dharmodayā*;
one should make it worshipped—that is, made radiant—by means of red flowers, that is, by the *rajas*.
Because it consists of great passion (*mahārāga*), the accomplishment of its great purpose occurs through this very [means].
Consequently, since the entire world, fallen into worldly passion, arises and perishes, it is appropriate to rely upon perfectly pure passion for the attainment of the supreme state.
Thus, the Master has also established that even the *karmamudrā* serves as a cause for stabilizing the mind.
And so it is said in the *Śrīhevajra*:
Just as those burnt by fire are again steamed by fire,
so too those burnt by the fire of passion are steamed by the fire of passion.
By the very same piece of poison by which all living beings die,
one who knows the true nature of poison may expel that poison with poison itself.
Just as bean-based food is given to one seized by wind,
and that very wind is overcome by wind through the application of contrary medicine.

Alternatively, one should cause the *dharmodayā* within the heart of the Vajradhara to be worshipped with a red flower by means of a mind of bliss accompanied by passion (*sarāga*), thereby making it radiant;
for such a distinguished state of mind arises even without the union with a consort, solely through the grace of the feet of a true guru.
And so says Daupāda:
Whether through the yoga of wisdom one suddenly attains the state of a Vajra-holder, or through that very yoga by means of awakening like the cool-rayed moon—
he who knows the empowerment is the Guru here, and no other.
The power of which strikes the mind instantly, like a wicked person.
Therefore, it is established that perfect accomplishment depends solely upon a mind of bliss.
And in the *Vajraḍāka*:
"Through difficult and intense observances, the body withers and becomes miserable."
The mind is distracted by suffering; from distraction, success is otherwise [prevented].

Alternatively, because it is a great elixir (*mahārāsa*yana), its production must necessarily be performed for the purpose of nasal administration (*nasya*) and for the sake of both non-existence and existence; and it is stated in that very same source:
"The great red [substance] with camphor is the most excellent elixir;
the great red flower is that which arises during the menstrual period."
Regarding the word *saṃllikhya*: the root *likh* means "to arrange letters.
The meaning is, "having made an arrangement in the form of imperishable syllables (*akṣara*)."
He asks, "With which? and replies: "With the ring finger. It is called the "ring finger" (*anāmikā*) because it does not bend (*na namati*);
and that is the *bola*.
By whom was he characterized? He says: "by the sixth Jina.
He was characterized by Kṛṣṇa Madana;
the sense is: through service to him.
The third case ending is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*). For example: "He saw the student by means of his water-pot" (*kamaṇḍalunā chātram adrākṣīt*).
[In the phrase] "having been recited three times," it is likewise.
That from which recitation (*japtaṃ jalpanam*) and absorption (*layaḥ*) arise through the non-emission—that is, the immobility—of the three, namely body, speech, and mind;
the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). And thus it is said:
"Even of sweetmeats, in every forest and on every path..."
Just as an elephant is made into a water-plaything by means of its arrangement.
Likewise, desiring to lead the elephant of the mind, the yogi cultivates the innate water-maiden,
passion, strength, and even the weak woman.
If the elephant of the mind is bound by means of molasses, rice-grains, and the like,
all fear has set, and even a profit of ten million remains stable.
By means of that, the practitioner may accomplish even the impossible for the sake of what is to be accomplished;
for through that gateway, even the mind—which is otherwise unachievable—is brought under control.
Also in the *Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana*:
"Having attained the drawn-in (or heated) Madana together with the Vidyā, [one experiences] the primordial bliss."
Only that much should be done so that the mind does not become distracted.
Just as a certain great medicine is both delicious and destructive of disease,
so too is the bliss of wisdom and skillful means, which effortlessly destroys the afflictions.
To everyone, a beautiful woman is a source of delight; yet to those whose passion is pure, she is a noose around the neck, while to others, she is a knife that cuts their bonds.

Alternatively, he explains with what kind of ring finger [one should perform this]: "by the sixth Jina. The instrumental case here expresses accompaniment; that is, it is accompanied by the sixth Jina, which is the *bodhicitta*.
The meaning is "united with the perfectly complete bodhicitta," because arising is dependent upon that;
[it is] "recited with the three syllables."
By means of the three syllables— the body, speech, and mind— when recited and brought to dissolution,
[the result follows] because of their non-distraction and lack of faltering.
And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
Recitation is said to be the act of speaking; it consists of the continuous utterance of the vowels and consonants. ||2||
Thereafter, having placed the right hand into the vessel of the Paramādya,
one should perform the vajra-sipping according to the instruction by touching it with the tongue.
He states another ritual action with the words "tadanu" and so forth.
The connection is that one should perform the *vajrasavana* (diamond purification).
It is called "vajra" because it is the cause for bringing about the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
By the word "vajra," the substance of the black yogin is designated, through the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause. *Savana* means bathing.
The root *ṣuñ* means "to press.
He asks, "What is to be done? and replies: "Having cast [it] into the lotus-hand."
The placement of the lotus-hands:
"the other than the right" means the left. To the question "Where?", he says: "in the vessel of the Supreme Primeval One."
The Supreme is supreme bliss; for its sake, there is the primordial intoxicant, such as honey-wine (mādhvī) and so forth,
in its vessel.
"According to the instruction" means without deviating from the instruction.
"From the touch of the body" means from the touching of the limbs with both hands.
The instruction here is as follows: first, taking only a drop the size of a bee, one should perform an ablution with the mantra of the Goddess or the three-syllabled mantra.
Then, with the gesture of embracing using both the left and right hands, one should touch the body—starting from the head down to the big toes—with the liquid clinging to the palms.

Alternatively, one should touch [the body] with the liquid substance using the thumb and ring finger of the right hand, while the left palm holds a five-petaled red lotus upon which reside the mantras of the six Yoginīs, who are themselves the very forms of the six Yoginīs.
The traditional teaching (āmnāya) is "touching the śaya" and "the touch of the śaya.

There is also another explanation: "vajra" is great bliss (mahāsukha); with that, the wise one should perform the "savana," meaning the bath; the sense is that he should make himself consist of great bliss.

The meaning is that there is a tasting with the *bodhicitta* of the *vajra*, that is, the *bola*; it refers to something held during practice even if it has slightly fallen. As for the question "Where?", he says: "In the vessel of the Paramādya."

The first vessel for that [reality] is the supreme, ineffable form, the *dharmodayā* (source of phenomena), because it sustains great bliss and because it serves as the support for all the Tathāgatas;
the meaning is that [the practitioner] is situated within that very support.
For it is precisely there that innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) arises.
And because for those possessing skillful means and wisdom, there is the severing of bondage in that very [state].
Thus it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"By whatever and by whatever the world is bound, by that very same thing one should release the bondage."
The world is deluded; it does not know reality, and being devoid of reality, it shall not attain accomplishment.
For by whatever fierce karma living beings are bound,
by that very same means, when applied with skillful method, they are liberated from the bondage of existence.
If this were so, it would be contradictory to say that innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) arises; for that which has arisen is by nature subject to constant destruction,
and that which is perishable is common to worldly pleasure.
Granted that this may be so, nevertheless there is no fault in adducing it as an illustration. As it has been said:
"A swan joined with mere whiteness is indeed given as a comparison for the moon;
likewise, even worldly pleasure, when presented, is inscribed upon the path of cognition."
And that which was to be established by the venerable Mahāguru regarding the association with the lotus—
that very thing, which is the resort for those who have no other resort, has also been made the ground for this illustration.

Awakening is not achieved through Sanskrit; even a distinguished foreign language may be a source of ridicule. Yet, the men of mountain-dwelling forest tribes are won over by means of words fashioned according to their own speech.
As the venerable Āryadeva said:
"Just as a barbarian cannot be made to understand by means of a different language,
so too the world cannot be made to understand without recourse to worldly conventions."
Furthermore, just as the birth, existence, and destruction of a son in a dream are experienced as causes of pleasure and pain, yet at dawn all of it is found to be false,
so too everything exists only during the time of practice.
But in the innate primordial gnosis (*ādijñāna*), it does not exist at all; thus, everything is perfectly sound.

Consequently, once the wings have been formed, like a bird the yogi desires to travel through the sky, yet even while experiencing a fall to the ground, he who possesses well-formed wings joined at a single point gradually brings even the expanse of the firmament under his own control by means of the Lord of Yogis. And so, in this precipice—
"One must remain vigilant.
And it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"One should practice with diligence so that no differentiation arises."
"Differentiation" refers to the separation of body, speech, and mind, as well as the slipping of the *bindu*.
Having done what? It says: "having cast the lotus-hand of the left.
This is because of the method of joining and opening the two petals of the lotus with the thumb and fingers of the left hand.
And it is also stated in the *Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana*:
"With the thumb and index finger of the hand, one should slowly perform the closing and opening of the two petals of the lotus, while the face of the blooming lotus quivers."

Alternatively, it means that which measures (māti) and discerns (paricchinatti) the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). "Supreme" (*paraṃ*) refers to the moment characterized by supreme consciousness, the *bodhicitta*. Its "first vessel" (*ādyaṃ pātraṃ*) is the "fragile one" (*bhiduraṃ*); having cast into that the "lotus-hand" (*karakamala*), meaning having placed the lotus of wisdom (*prajñāpadma*)—which, like a hand, is endowed with qualities such as being hairless and so forth.
And it is said in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*: "..."
"One should form a lotus with the palms of the hands," as it is said.
Also, in the *Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana*: "One should form a lotus with the palms of the hands, and likewise with the two armpits."

The intended meaning is that he himself, seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), should place the *nāyikā* upon his body; or alternatively, since there is no external consort (*bāhyamudrā*), the "lotus-hand" (*karakamala*) refers to the hand itself, and the meaning is that he should cause it to blossom with his very own hand—
not only the lotus-hand, but specifically the left arm as well as the right.
"And having cast" means having internalized; the word "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

Furthermore, this twofold stabilization of the drop (*bindu*) by means of the great medicine of the great bliss of emission (*cyavana-mahāsukha*) and so forth is possible even for those who possess impure passion.

Or how could that which is of an uninterrupted nature and consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) arise within the ritual partner (*karmāṅganā*)? As it has been said: "If those three worlds were to experience perishable pleasure (*kṣarasukha*) all at once, even then they would not obtain even a ten-millionth part of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*)."
Since that which is produced from causes characterized by lightness possesses momentary destruction and the quality of causing suffering,
how could the Lord of True Bliss be established by such means?
To this doubt, he says: "By touching sleep according to instruction.
Sleep (*śaya*) is slumber, the cessation of the cognitive faculties (*vijñānendriya*), which means not wandering toward other objects but being fixed on one point alone.
"From contact with that" means from directing one's attention toward it.
Alternatively, *śaya* means sleep; because of its similarity to that, death is so designated.

Death, moreover, is a state of meditation (*dhyāna*) characterized by the cessation of the vital breath (*vāyu*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the sense organs (*indriya*); "from contact with that" means from directing one's attention toward that [state].
As it is said in the Śrī Hevajra:
"That bliss by which death occurs here is called meditative absorption (dhyāna),
because a slight death is of a false nature."
As it is said in the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara: "That which is called death is this conceptual construction; it is led to the state of Khecarī."
In this regard, the instruction is also stated:
"If the breath is moving, the bitten spot is unsurpassed great bliss."
By that very means, taking refuge is the remedy and the counter-action.
Either directly experiencing or mentally visualizing the abundance of happiness previously enjoyed,
one should cultivate the attainment of desire with a mind directed inward.
And in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"For the entire world is meditated upon by the mind, yet it is not meditated upon;
the thorough knowledge of all phenomena is meditation, and indeed no meditation at all."
Among those, there is one supreme state beyond which nothing exists: the great bliss that is self-cognized.
From self-cognition comes accomplishment, for self-cognition is indeed the meditative cultivation.
And so it is said:
"While enjoying great bliss, sleep with consciousness, objects, and senses;
treat conceptualizations of praise, blame, fame, and gain as if they were a mere hut."
If this practice of Bhusuka is performed within the mind,
then it will easily strike down the currents of the tranquil mind.
This has been graciously set forth by Bhusukapāda:
even while sleeping, one’s dwelling is nowhere [else]; it is accomplished—let it be awaited. ||3||
Having performed the *karanyāsa* by joining the thumbs and fingers of both hands, one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* with the six mantras of Vīreśvarī. ||4||
He states another ritual act: "having performed," and so forth.
The connection is that one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* (placement of mantras on the limbs).
By what means? He says: "by the six *Vīreśvarī* mantras."
The six yoginīs—Vajravārāhī, Yāminī, Mohinī, Sañcālanī, Santrāsanī, and Caṇḍikā—are known as the heroic sovereigns; [they are invoked] by their six mantras.
Therein, this is the ritual placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*): *Oṃ vaṃ* at the navel.
Hoṃ yoṃ at the heart; hrīṃ moṃ at the throat; hreṃ hrīṃ at the mouth.
HŪṂ HŪṂ at the head;
PHAṬ PHAṬ as the weapon on all limbs. Having thus performed the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa).
First, having performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*):
"By the joining of the thumb and fingers" means by joining them starting from the thumb of the left hand and proceeding through the fingers up to the little finger.
The sequence there is as follows: *oṃ vaṃ* on the thumb.
Hoṃ yoṃ on the index finger; hrīṃ moṃ on the middle finger;
hreṃ hrīṃ on the ring finger.
HŪṂ HŪṂ at the little fingers;
PHAṬ PHAṬ at the tips of all the fingers;
and [PHAṬ] at the bases of all [the fingers]—this is the traditional teaching.
There is also another explanation: the connection is that "one should perform the *aṅganyāsa*.
*Aṅga* refers to the downward vital air (*apānavāyu*).
To the question "by what?", he says: "by the mantras of Vīreśvarī."
The Hero is the syllable *Ha*, in the form of Śrī Heruka, abiding in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*);
his Mistress is the Blessed Lady in the form of Caṇḍālī, abiding in the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*);
[the practice is performed] with her mantras.
Because of protecting through reflection (*manana*),
by means of mantras as methods;
"by six" refers to these.
By means of the sixfold methods beginning with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*);
or else, the instrumental case in "by the six" (*ṣaḍbhiḥ*) is used in the sense of accompaniment,
meaning that one should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) together with these six.
And so it has been said: "Withdrawal of the senses, meditation, breath control, concentration, recollection, and absorption— this is held to be the six-limbed yoga."
And so it is stated in the *Śrī Kālacakra*:

"The Lord of Jinas is the withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), which is tenfold; Akṣobhya is indeed the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the Sword-bearer (*Khaḍgin*) is the breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which is again tenfold; and Ratnapāṇi is the retention (*dhāraṇā*)."
Through the *ḍombī* there is recollection (*anusmṛti*), and likewise the Holder of the Lotus (*kamaladhara*) and the Glorious Samādhi (*śrīsamādhi*) are the Wheel-Holder (*cakrin*).
Each one is further divided into five types, since they are indeed distinguished by the vowels and consonants beginning with *a* and *ka*.
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the non-functioning of the ten sense objects and their corresponding subjects within the body;
wisdom (prajñā), reasoning (tarka), deliberation (vicāra), delight (rati), and unshakable bliss (acala-sukha) are meditation (dhyāna), which is also one-pointedness of mind (ekacitta).
Breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the two paths; its faltering occurs when the vital breath enters the middle channel.
Indeed, the entry of the vital breath into the bindu, the cessation of both outward and inward movements, concentration, and one-pointedness of mind [constitute the practice].
The vision of the Caṇḍālī that indeed occurs within the body and in space is the recollection (anusmṛti);
through the power of the non-emitted bliss consisting of wisdom and means, there is meditative absorption (samādhi) in the image of gnosis.

This practice of the Sustainer of the Universe may be threefold according to the distinctions of "soft" (mṛdu) and so forth; there are three mudrās, each with three measures, corresponding to the three types of movement: the physical, the mental, and the divine.
Having done what? He says: "having performed the placement of the hand" (*pravidhāya karanyāsam*).
The "hand" (*kara*) is the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), so called because it takes (*rāti*) or seizes (*guṇhāti*) the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*);
the meaning is that one has performed its placement by forceful entry into the central path (*madhyamāmārga*).
And likewise in that very same [text]:

"That power which proceeds from the center of the navel to the supreme state, to the end of the twelve [fingers] and the end of the digits (kalā), is firmly restrained at the navel; resembling lightning and fire, it rises in the form of a staff."
Moving with a soft and graceful gait from one cakra to the next, she is impelled through the central channel until,
by force, she touches the aperture of the uṣṇīṣa like a needle piercing the outer skin.
At that time, by means of supreme force, one should propel the downward breath (āpāna) along the upward path;
having pierced the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa), it proceeds to the city of the Supreme [Brahman] when the pair of winds is restrained.
Thus, through the awakening of the vajra within the mind from its objects, one attains the state of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
Furthermore, this Viśvamātā of the yogins has the five superknowledges as her essential nature.
To the question "Why should it be performed?", he says: "From the union of the *vṛddhāṅguṣṭha* and the *aṅgulī*.
The *vṛddhāṅguṣṭha* is the *vajra*, being both "grown" (*vṛddha*) and the "thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*); that is the *bola*.
It is called *aṅgulī* because it "dissolves into the body" (*aṅge līyate*); [here] *śukra* [is meant], with a reversal of syllables according to etymological rules (*nairukta*).
The meaning is that from those two comes union (*samāyoga*), which is non-falling (*askhalana*). This is the instruction regarding the word *Vīreśvarī*.
The meaning is written as follows: from the letter *ū* comes upward movement; from the letter *ī* comes the agitation of the wind;
the letter *r* is a line consisting of fire; and *Īśvarī* [is so called] because of all happiness.

This, however, is the causal Caṇḍālī in the form of the objective support (*ālambana*); because she is of the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), she bestows the bliss of the vibration (*spanda*) arising from the mudrā.
Our teachers maintain that she is raised up precisely for the purpose of raising the *bindu*.
That very point is now established for those who delight in analogies:
A lotus placed upon an equal vessel, its interior illuminated by a lamp,
stands with the base of its inverted lid resting upon the head.
In reality, however, yogis must fall [into] that very state which is innate in form, flowing spontaneously, and bestowing the bliss of vibration (*spanda*).
As it is said: "The protection of the *bodhicitta* within the six limbs is the mild stage; the movement of vibration is the middling stage."
The movement of the flowless state is merely the highest limit.
Thus, the action-seal (karmamudrā) bestows the bliss of emission,
while the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) bestows the bliss of vibration.
"Mahāmudrā bestows the bliss of the motionless.
And it has been said:
"Firm like a young crab or a ripe plantain fruit..."
Arising from the existence of a cause that is without a counter-cause,
she manifests in the form of the fruit.
By means of the instruction of Caṇḍālī, she alone is the one who revels in great bliss;
she is the goddess Nairātmikā, and she is Vajravairocanī.

Thereafter, it is explained by excluding the *caṇḍālī* interpretation—the connection being that "one should perform the *aṅganyāsa*. *Aṃ*: the Goddess in the form of the letter *a*, residing in the *nirmāṇacakra*. *Gaṃ*: "he goes," thus *aṅga* is the *apāna* wind.
One should perform its *nyāsa*, which is its contraction and upward lifting.
Having performed what? He says: "having performed the *karanyāsa*.
Because the hand is twofold, the word "hand" (*kara*) here denotes the two arms (or the two winds).
The meaning is: having performed its placement (nyāsa) and cessation (nirodha).
And so it is said in the Śrī Hevajra:
"The mandala is the footprint; because of its being rubbed (malanāt), it is called a mandala."
The snapping of the hands and likewise the clenching of the fingers constitutes the mudrā;
otherwise, laxity of the apāna wind would arise.
By this, it is indicated that the two aforementioned arms (or winds) must be drawn in and introduced into great bliss;
for the accomplishment of the goal occurs through the stabilization of the winds alone.

As it is said in the *Śrī Kālacakra*: "The entry of the vital breath into the center, the binding of the movements of the sun and moon in the right and left [channels], the mind engaged with the consort, and the awakening of the vajra through supreme bliss."

The sound of a vajra upon a lotus, or the splashing of water from one's own hands, for the sake of bliss; the non-abandonment of the seed-syllable accompanied by bliss—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru, which removes the fear of death.
And so it is said:
From the vital breath comes longevity, from the drop comes the body, and from the perfectly steady mind comes liberation;
the union of these three is proclaimed as the "triplet" (tripuṭī).
He states why it must be performed: "by the union of the thumb and finger of the elder" (*vṛddhāṅguṣṭhāṅgulisamāyogāt*).
That which abides in the limb (*aṅga*) is the "thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*), namely the *vajra*;
this is an etymological alteration of the phonemes (*nairukta-varṇaviparyaya*).
The "old thumb" is the intense *bola*;
the fingers are the semen (*śukra*). From their union comes the "slipping" (*skhalana*), and from that [it arises]. And it is said:
"For him upon whose embrace the moon falls, how can there be happiness?"
When the spring has arrived, by what cause does the mango tree's bud fall away as fruit?
And so it is said:
"The fool whose moon of wisdom sinks into the lotus of attachment seeks its fruit by tearing apart the garland of flowers."
Also in the *Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana*:
"One should churn the ocean of the lotus out of a desire for the innate nectar."
"And so that the poison of dispassion does not arise"—
"by the six" means characterized by or accompanied by the six consciousnesses, beginning with the visual consciousness.
He asks, "By what kind [of means]? and says: "By the mantras of Vīreśvarī.

Vīra is the Blessed One; his Īśvarī is Śūnyatā (Emptiness). She herself is the *mantra* because she protects through contemplation (*manana*). Those [means] for which she is the *mantra*, i.e., the method (*upāya*), are by those [means].
Alternatively, it is by the mantras—the methods—of Vīreśvarī, Śūnyatā, because she arises having taken them as her very object. ||4||
Thereafter, one should slowly sprinkle the vessel—produced from the union with the raktāruṇā consort upon the Vajradhara—with the well-purified juices of serpents contained within a cloth. ||5||
He states another injunction: "And thereafter," and so forth.
The word *ca* has the sense of "again.
The connection is that one should scatter—that is, sprinkle—the vessel (*amatram*).
Regarding the phrase "born from the union of raṅga and aruṇa":
*raṅga* is tin (*vaṅga*), and *aruṇa* is copper (*tāmra*); the meaning is that bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) is produced from their union, that is, their combination.
"Even" (*samam*) means equal, being free from blemishes, roughness, croaking, and so forth;
the intended meaning is "like a mirror.
To the question "With what should one scrape it?", he says: "With things born of serpents" (*bhujagabhavaiḥ*).
"Bhujaga" means a snake or lead; "born from that" refers to those [leaves] made from it.
"Extremely pure" means devoid of leaf-marks. "Situated on cloth" means [the letters] placed upon a piece of fabric.
"By those [fingers] upon that smooth *sicaya* cloth"—meaning "slowly.

The intention is as follows: having fashioned a swing from a red cloth by placing the fingers with light steps, and having applied vermilion (*sindūra*) there, one should move it slightly in sequence with the finger.
He asks, "Where? and says: "Above the Vajradhara.

This means above the vessel (*pātra*) that holds the *vajra*—that is, the vessel accompanied by the *madana*. There is also another interpretation: the connection is that one should scatter the vessel (*amatra*) [upon it].

*Amatra* means that which protects from disease—the suffering consisting of the four hundred and four types of illnesses. Alternatively, *amatra* refers to the vessel whose nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), because it serves as the support for all things. One should scatter—that is, join—that [substance] with it.
"Equal" (*sama*) means because it is of a single nature everywhere.
"Born from the union of *raṅga* and *aruṇa*":
*raṅga* is *bodhicitta* because of its whiteness or because of its being possessed of passion (*saraṅga*); *aruṇa* is Amitābha, which is *rajas*.
From their union, that [state] is born.
Where should it be applied? He says: "Upon Vajradhara.
*Vajra* means the thunderbolt; he who holds that very thing is *vajradhara*, [the one] on all sides.
Because it is accessible and because it is a precipice situated above that which has been born, he asks with whom one should scatter [it]; he says: "by those born of serpents.
A *bhujaga* is a snake; by the poisons (*viṣa*) originating from them—since sense objects (*viṣaya*) themselves are poison due to being the cause of misfortune—one should scatter [them].
And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"These [objects] that are to be enjoyed must be enjoyed after they have been rendered free of poison through purification.
And likewise in that same [text]:
In the same way, the jewel of cyclic existence, endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure,
becomes poison when impure, but becomes like nectar when purified.
By what kind [of things]? By those that are perfectly pure.
These objects, too, are by their very nature of the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
However, because they arise like poison through the power of ignorance, they are [rendered harmless] by those [means] thoroughly purified through their innate function (*sahajavṛtti*).
"Contained within cloth" (*sicayagataiḥ*) means being enclosed as if tied within a piece of cloth (*karpaṭa*).
"Gradually" means with composure;
or else, it refers to the red dyes produced from the *sihlaka* plant, which is a type of snake—
[the word] "together with" (*saha*) being understood as the ellipsis.

The sense is that even worldly passion (*laukikarāga*) should be cast aside therein. Alternatively, it means "by means of *sindūra*s"— that is, by means of the essence of great passion (*mahārāgarasa*)— because of their being full of redness (*sarāgatva*), like *sindūra* produced from serpents.
The meaning is that one should scatter [the flowers]. ||5||
There, having carefully drawn a wheel with a peacock-feather tip as the heart of the Jina’s heart,
one should inscribe the row of mantras within its center using a probe made of gold.
He states another duty with the words "Therein," and so forth.
The connection is that one should draw the *mantrālī*, the sequence of mantras, of the Blessed Lady.
Having done what? He says: "having drawn the wheel."
Regarding the phrase "the heart of the hearts of the Jinas":
the Jinas are the four Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the others; of them...
The heart is the Blessed One Śrī Heruka, whose essential nature is Akṣobhya; his heart, in turn, is the Source of Phenomena (dharmodayā),
which is its true nature.
Regarding the term *śikhikoṭikam*: *śikhi* means fire; because it has three [flames], there are exactly three *koṭis*.
The suffix *kan* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). The meaning is "the triangle of the wheel."
Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*), it refers to the mirror dusted with vermilion powder.
To the question of where the mantra-line should be written, he says: "within that" (*tadgarbhe*).
This means within the womb of the *dharmodaya* drawn upon the surface of the mirror.
He states with what [instrument] it should be written: "with a golden stylus" (*gāṅgeyaśalākayā*).
It should be understood from the subsequent verse or from oral instruction that it is to be written with the left hand using a stylus made of *gāṅgeya*, which is gold.

Herein is the traditional practice (*āmnāya*): first, the Blessed Lady Dharmodayā, in the form of the syllable *vaṃ* accompanied by the moon, the bindu, and the nāda, is to be written upon the filaments (*kiñjalka*).

Thereafter, in the center of the *dharmodayā*, one should write the King of Mantras of the Blessed Lady, arising from the extraction of the mantra by means of three rows of syllables numbering fifteen— corresponding to the directions of Smara and Śaṅkara— which represent the purity of body, speech, and mind. By means of the letters *ha* and *ā*, which are the essential nature of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady as they manifest both wheels (*cakras*), and by all the remaining syllables produced in the form of the letter *ha*,
it should be written below [the seed-syllable] upon the letter *vaṃ*, through the purity of non-duality.
Alternatively, having placed the syllable *oṃ* in the filaments, three [syllables] should be written on the sides by means of the very line of the *dharmodayā*.
There is also the tradition of some that the syllable *vaṃ* is to be placed in the center.
There is another explanation as well: "therein" means one should write the row of mantras, the *avadhūtī*, within the *dharmodayā*.

The meaning is that one should establish [it] in the form of syllables (*akṣara*). Because they protect the mind, they are *mantras*; because they have the wind as their companion, they are *bindus*. Since these proceed to the wheel of bliss (*sukhacakra*), the *avadhūtī* itself is designated by the term *mantrālī*—meaning a row, a bridge, or a path.
By what [means] is it written in the sky?
He says [it is] "with a probe made of gold from the Gaṅgā" (gāṅgeya-śalākayā).

It goes to the earth (gām), which is the source of phenomena (dharmodayā); thus it is the Gaṅgā, the stream of nectar falling from the peak of Mount Sumeru. The drops produced from that are "made of gold from the Gaṅgā" (gāṅgeya-bindavaḥ), because it is precisely from its flow that those peaks of jewels arise.
Those very drops, traveling by that path, are like "sticks" (śalākā) because they enter the hollow of the *avadhūtī* and proceed through it. Having done what? He says: "the wheel," and so forth.
The Jina is Śrī Heruka; his heart is the wheel (cakra) known as Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), because it arises there at all times.
Having drawn that, one should visualize it in that form—this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "peaked like a crest of a peacock" (*śikhikoṭika*):
*Śikhī* means a flame; *caṇḍālī* means its tip or foremost part. The sense is that this [tip] is on the head (*ke*) of the letter *va*, because [the letter *va*] is facing downwards.
"Within its womb" means precisely within the midst of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Alternatively, one should write the line of mantras and offer a stream of drops (*bindu*).
He asks, "With what? and replies: "With the Ganges-reed.
A drop is *gāṅgeya*;
for the purpose of its movement, it is like a reed, thus a "reed" (*śalākā*), which is the *avadhūtī*. With that [reed].
Having done what? He says: "having correctly depicted the heart of the heart of the Jina.
The Jina is Śrī Heruka; his heart is the syllable, which is the *bodhicitta*; its heart is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). The meaning is that one should place that properly within the mind.
"The wheel" (*cakra*)— [End of excerpt]
Because it cuts through all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

"Having the peak of fire" (*śikhikoṭika*) means that which has the peak—the tip or supreme form—of fire (*śikhin*); it is so called because it burns the fuel of ignorance and because of its extreme sharpness. (6)
On the outer portion of the wheel, in the directions of the east, north, west, and south,
one should draw six svastikas in sequence with the left hand.
He states the specific detail: "of the wheel," and so forth. One should draw the coils distinguished by six svastikas. As to where one should draw them, he says: "on the outer part of the wheel."
Outside the *dharmodayā* [triangle], because there are many possible locations even there, he states the certainty: "in the directions of the east, north, west, and the descendant of the Sun.
The descendant of the Sun (*ārkī*) is Yama.
Regarding the phrase "in sequence":
it means in the order of the east, north, and so forth; "with the left hand" is self-evident.
There is also another explanation: *sat* means existing; those for whom there is a truly good *svastika*—that is, happiness—are the *svastikas*, which are the *bindus*.
The connection is that one should "draw" and "arrange" them.
To the question of where one should arrange them, he says: "on the outer part of the wheel," meaning on the exterior portion of the *mahāsukhacakra*.
Of what nature is it? It is that which has the eastern, northern, western, and southern directions as its very location;
the meaning is "in every atom" and "in every pore.
By what was it written? He says: "by the hand," that is, by the wind.
The winds residing in the body are grasped because they are represented by the five fingers.
By what kind [of finger]?
By the left, which is charming.
The meaning is "without distraction. To the question "How should one scratch? he says: "Gradually and with great steadiness," because of its immovability.
Or [it may be performed] according to the sequence of each individual pore. ||7||

Having drawn forth the Vajra Goddess, caused her to enter, and bound her within the syllables of the mantra, one should satisfy her according to the ritual procedure by reciting "jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ. ||8||
He states another procedure, beginning with "having drawn in" and so forth.
The connection is that one should satisfy the Vajra Goddess.
Having done what? He says: "having drawn in."

Having drawn the Goddess residing in the Akaniṣṭha realm by means of the syllable *jaḥ*, using rays in the form of hooks emanating from the garland of the Goddess’s mantra inscribed upon the surface of a mirror;
[and] having caused her to enter— meaning, having caused her to enter into the letters of the mantra inscribed on the surface of the mirror by means of the syllable *hūṃ*.
"Having bound" means: having bound it with the syllable *vaṃ* within those very mantra-syllables, making it well-fastened.
To explain how the summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) should be performed, he says: "having recited *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*."

The meaning is that one should recite these root mantras individually for each [deity], preceded by meditation, according to the sequence of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), causing entry (*praveśana*), and binding (*bandhana*).
"By means of the ritual procedure" (*vidhānāt*) means this.
