Performing the *jvālāmudrā* and other gestures,
the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) states: "With feet stepped forward and the gaze directed upward, one should [utter] the sound of *pheṃ* from the head."
There is also another explanation: one should satisfy the Vajradevī, that is, Caṇḍālī, by making her nourished. Regarding the word "having drawn" (ākṛṣya):
even though she has gone upward, [one draws] the fallen stream of nectar.
The meaning is "having caused [it] to bow.
Regarding "having caused it to enter into the syllables of the mantra":
the mantra is the *bodhicitta*; the meaning is that having caused it to be included within the syllables—which are the gnoses of great bliss—it is to be perfected in their form.

The intention is that since it is improper for her, once she has been perfected, to remain in the form of a cause, it is appropriate that she be the innate Caṇḍālī herself. "And having bound" means having made her firmly bound within great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"By the rule" means according to the naming [of the syllables]. He clarifies this very point by stating: "Having recited *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*."
The meaning is: having brought [the reality] face-to-face through the sequence endowed with the meaning of these four syllables. ||8||

Thereafter, one should perform various forms of worship for her, who is the very embodiment of mantra, with foods to be chewed, swallowed, licked, drunk, and sucked, possessing all desirable qualities. (9)
He states the worship with the words "tadanu" and so forth.
The connection is that immediately after that, one should perform—that is, carry out—her *saparyā*, which is to say, her *pūjā* (worship).
[The phrase] "of the one whose form is mantra" [is used].
Of her whose form is the mantra unified like milk and water.
"Vividha" means of various kinds.
"By edibles" (bhakṣyaiḥ) means by flour-cakes and the like;
"by foods" (bhojyaiḥ) means by grains;
"by lickables" (lehyaiḥ) means by honey and so forth.
"By drinks and so forth" means by beverages such as *pānaka* and the like;
"by things to be sucked" means by mangoes and the like;
"with the qualities of desire" means with the enjoyment of the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).

There is also another explanation: one should cultivate single-minded devotion through the constant practice of the worship of that Goddess. "In the form of mantra" means in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
He states by what causes [this occurs]: "By means of those very [pleasures] being sprinkled upon [the senses], they become strengthened with power; and from that power, pleasure arises.
Thus, it is said: "by means of the qualities of desire."
The meaning is that one should even engage in the enjoyment of the five objects of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) without attachment.
Alternatively, since there are thirteen "desires" (*kāma*) and three "qualities" (*guṇa*), the term *kāmaguṇa* refers to the sixteen transitions of the vital winds (*pavana*).
The intention is that by means of this daily contemplation, through the mastery of the breath, they are gradually absorbed into the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) itself. ||9||
With various forces accompanied by intoxication, with five most excellent offerings, and with songs, instrumental music, dances, circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise; || 10 ||
He says "not only by these" and so forth, beginning with "by various" (*vividhaiḥ*).
"By forces" (*balaiḥ*) means by meats; "by various" means by many kinds of *gokudaha* (human corpses).
"With offerings" means accompanied by ritual substances;
"with five offerings" means with the five types of offerings.
With the most excellent and supreme songs, namely the vajra-songs; "with others" refers to those that are very graceful.
With musical instruments such as the lute and flute,
with dances performed with vajra-steps,
and with circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise.
[He is worshipped] with circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns.
There is also another explanation regarding the term "with forces" (*balaiḥ*):

[it refers to the forces] whose nature is that of the *gokudana* [seeds]. From those known as Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya—which consist of the five aggregates—there is also [absorption] into their Great Bliss.
Because it is included therein.
Regarding the term "samadana": that which intoxicates is *madana*.

"With the syllable *ṅ* together with those" means with those [syllables] accompanied by it. "Offerings" (*upahāra*) refers to the sense objects (*viṣaya*), because the universe is assisted—that is, honored—by them.
"By five" refers to the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness and so forth.
"By the most excellent [qualities] such as hatred" means by those characterized by the sounds and resonances arising from great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"By musical instruments" means by the sounds of the vajra;
"by dances" means by the graceful movements of the limbs during sexual union;
"by circumambulation" means by the clockwise turning movements of the vajra-lotus.
"Prostration" (praṇati) means having one's gaze lowered through meditative concentration;
"praise" (nuti) refers to the utterance of sounds such as *hā* and *sī*.
Alternatively, the meaning is that [the practice is performed] together with all of these.
Because all [the causes] are of an identical nature with respect to that effect. ||10||
Desiring her accomplishment, one should perform the prescribed ritual of worship on the tenth lunar day, whether daily, every fortnight, or monthly. (11)
Thus concludes the procedure for external worship in the attainment of the knowledge of reality.
He states when it should be performed: "Every day," and so forth.
The connection is that one should perform the ritual of worship as previously described.
Regarding the word "asyā" (of this):
Of the goddess who is the form of mantra: daily means constantly; every fortnight refers to the tenth day of both the bright and dark lunar phases;
"every month" refers to the tenth day of the dark fortnight.
Because the Yoginī has authority specifically during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
Regarding the phrase "on the tenth lunar day" (tithau daśamyām):
the meaning is that the tenth day itself is the festival day of the Goddess.

"But that wise one, desiring accomplishment" means he who longs for mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*laukikalokottarasiddhi*). There is also another explanation: one should perform the aforementioned ritual of worship for this [goddess] whose nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"Every day" means "with every perception," since a day consists of perceptions;
the meaning is that whatever is perceived, one should cause that to enter into great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
"Counter-position" means either the position of existence or the position of non-existence.
"Month by month" means:
Because a month consists of two fortnights, the intended meaning is that one should apply both fortnights to great bliss (*mahāsukha*). And it was said by the Blessed One:
"A bodhisattva should rely on the meaning and not rely on the letter.
Thus, "desiring accomplishment" means wishing for accomplishment. To the question "Where? he says: "In the tenth [stage]."
The meaning is: "desiring mastery over the ten stages on the tenth stage. Regarding the phrase "on the lunar day":
the tenth stage itself is the goddess's lunar day (*tithi*), because she is always present there. ||11||
The Ritual for External Worship from the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhipañjikā*, composed by the Great Paṇḍita and Bhikṣu Vīryaśrīmitra of the illustrious Vikramaśīla Mahāvihāra.
[Now, the procedure for meditation:

Then, having completed the ritual of external worship, the one of vast compassion, who has destroyed his enemies, should meditate upon the Goddess previously described within the lotus of his heart, in the orb of the sun situated in the center of that heart. (1)
"Then," and so forth. The connection is that immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
"As previously described" means:
as possessing a physical form (*vigrahavatī*), having an innate nature (*sahajarūpiṇī*), as set forth earlier, or as taught by the Blessed One in the *Śrīsaṃvarārṇava* and other *pūrvatantras*.
"Having performed the ritual of external worship" means one by whom the ritual of worship has indeed been performed externally upon the surface of a mirror;
"of great compassion" means...
He whose compassion and mercy are vast and great—wherein does he meditate? To this he says: "In the lotus situated in the center of the created enemy."
In the lotus at the center of the *nirmāṇacakra*:
"the orb of the sun [of] the deceased heart.
One whose vital breaths (*asavaḥ*)—that is, the life-forces (*prāṇāḥ*)—have departed is "deceased" (*vyasuḥ*), meaning one who is dead.

His heart is a "lifeless heart" (vyasuhṛdaya); in that [heart], there is the orb (bimba) or mandala of the "hot-rayed one" (uṣṇagu), meaning the sun, which resides within the solar mandala located in the heart of the deceased.
There is also another explanation: one should meditate upon the Goddess.
She is called a goddess (*devī*) because she plays with the essence of great passion (*mahārāga*).
"As previously mentioned" has already been explained. As for what kind of person [the practitioner] is, he says: "having performed the rite of external worship."
Alternatively, she is called *vāhyā* because she is carried (*uhyate*); that is, the *avadhūtī*.
Or, she is the *karmamudrā* because she is an external woman (*bāhyāṅganā*).
He by whom the ritual of worship toward the external [consort] has been performed, resulting in the arising of bliss, is thus described.
Regarding the term *urukaruṇa*: *ka* means happiness (*sukha*), and that which obstructs (*ruṇaddhi*) this is *karuṇā*, namely the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
He who possesses vast (*uru*) or great (*mahatī*) compassion is *urukaruṇa*.

To the question "Where should one meditate?", it is said: "In the three-petaled wheel of the lotus in the center of the emanated enemy. Here, *nirmitāri* refers to the *dharmodayā*, which is both the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) and the mind-created enemy—that is, the three-petaled wheel.
In the lotus in the center of that [maṇḍala]:
"on the heart of the corpse and the orb of the sun" means on the solar disc at the heart of the corpse.
The meaning is: "the light of gnosis arisen from the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). And so it is said:
"Because the realm of phenomena is indeed devoid of self and is pure, it is like a sleeping corpse or an empty palace;
that which is without substrate is the perfectly pure form for the sake of realization."
That [is placed] upon the heart of the corpse.

The mandala of the sun, consisting of wisdom, heat, and light, pure and of fierce splendor—therein has arisen this [Goddess], whose nature is the perfectly pure dharmadhātu, the single form of the entire world. (1)

She whose complexion is the color of vermilion at twilight, who with the mass of her rays has cast away the luster of seven suns; who holds in her right hand a scimitar that destroys all afflictions and flashes with immeasurable brilliance;
and who bears in her left hand a most white lotus adorned with a banner filled with blood.
Her head is encircled by the Kālyā and Dambholikālyā, and her hands are raised upward and released. ||2||
He states the meditation (*bhāvanā*), beginning with "at twilight" (*sandhyā*) and so forth.

One should meditate upon her whose color is like that of twilight and vermilion because she consists of perfectly pure passion (*rāga*); the phrase "one should meditate upon her" is to be supplied from the context.

"Kharakara," and so forth. "Khara" means sharp; "karanikara" means a multitude of rays. By that [multitude], the splendor of the seven Arkas—that is, of the seven suns—is "apāstā," meaning cast away or dispelled by her; she is thus described. Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is the "Kartrī," the "Vidhātrī," and the "Sarvārtihantrī."
That which cuts through all suffering; "radiating immeasurable compassion" means radiating immeasurable...
She whose limit is her brilliance and luster;
with her left arm—that is, with her right arm—[she holds].
Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is bearing a lotus and holding a skull-cup.
"Excessively cool" means stainless.
"Filled with blood" means being filled with the blood of the four Māras.
"With the left hand" means with the left arm.
"Adorned with a banner" means holding a khaṭvāṅga staff on her left side.
"With head encircled" means...
"Whose head is followed? He says: "By Dambholikālī.
*Dambholi* itself is *dambholikā*.
The suffix *kan* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), meaning "a row of thunderbolts.
Of what nature is she? She is Kālī, that is, the Black One; and by whom [is she so described]?
By one whose head is adorned with a garland of skulls (*kapālāvalī*) due to [her] instruction.
Thus it should be understood.
"Ka" means the head; or, it refers to one whose head is surrounded by its row—that is, the row of [deities].
In this interpretation, the instruction is that the vajra-garland is black.

Regarding the phrase *muktamūrdhvotthahastām*: it means she whose hands are raised upward in such a way that they are released [from the hair]. Alternatively, it may mean she whose right hand (*dakṣiṇakara*) is slightly attached to the ends of her mass of hair (*keśakalāpa*), which is loosened and raised upward. ||2||
Her limbs adorned with a garland of severed heads, with blood flowing from her mouth, tasting it with relish, and uttering loud roars;
with a jackal’s face above on her left, and faces of Wrath at the base of her primary face;
full of bliss, full of passion, endowed with various aesthetic sentiments (rasas), she dances in the half-lotus posture.
Her limbs were sealed with mudrās; she was divested of clothing, sixteen years of age, and possessed of excellent form.
He states another qualification: "muṇḍālī" and so forth. [It refers to her] whose body is adorned with a garland of human heads, and from whose mouth blood flows.
She from whose lotus-like mouth blood flows—that is, red blood—is "one whose mouth has flowing blood.
This is either due to the onset of her menses (*mahārajas*) or because she drinks the blood of the four Māras;
thus, [the phrase] *svādagum* [is used].
*svādaḥ* means taste,
and that is of six kinds.
She whose eyes are the six tastes themselves is thus [described].
"Facing forward" is because she has three eyes. "Emitting sounds" means emitting the sound produced by great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "With a hideous face" means having the face of a boar.
He asks "Where? and replies: "On the left" means on the right side;
"upwards" is an adverbial modifier;
and so forth, beginning with "excellent and auspicious."

She whose face—the primary source—is characterized by even a slight, excellent, distinguished, fortunate, and captivating anger, and who has another face, namely the face of a boar; she is such [a woman].
Or, "tām" may be taken as the accusative singular.
"With bliss" means immersed in innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). "With passion" means consisting of great passion (*mahārāga*).
"Endowed with various sentiments" means possessing the nine dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others,
because it pacifies all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*).
"Ardhaparyaṅkanṛtyām" means dancing in the half-lotus posture,
because her purpose has been accomplished.

"Her limbs are sealed by the mudrās" means that her body is properly sealed (*mudrita*) by the five *sāṃvarī* mudrās, which consist of the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*), the bracelet (*rucaka*), the earrings (*kuṇḍala*), the crest-jewel (*śiromaṇi*), and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). And thus it is said in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*:
"Adorned with a necklace, a breast-ornament, earrings, and a crest-jewel;
the sacred thread and ashes—these are proclaimed as the six mudrās.
Such is the tradition: these same [mudrās], excluding the ashes, are to be understood as the five mudrās of the Goddess.
And likewise, in the sādhana of Śabara-pāda as well, it says: "adorned with the five mudrās."
The *cakrikā* and the *mekhalā* are to be understood as the *upamudrās*.

Regarding the reading "her limbs are sealed by the six *mudrās*," since the *mekhalā* is included within the five *mudrās* explained here, the six *mudrās* are to be understood [as follows]: [the two] *mudrās*... [or] the single *mudrā*...
The compound "ṣaṇmudrāṣaṭ" should be understood as a genitive tatpuruṣa (possessive) compound. In either case, regarding the sixth Tathāgata, one must rely solely upon the lineage of gurus.
"Vyapagatavasanām" means naked, because she is devoid of the two coverings.
"Ṣoḍaśābdām" means sixteen years of age.
Because he is like the moon complete with its sixteen digits, or because he consists of the sixteenfold bliss;
as it is said in the *Śrī Kālacakra*:

By means of which the Holder of Wisdom (Prajñādhṛk) has placed upon his head this bliss of seminal emission and detachment; [he has placed] in the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the unchanging supreme bliss full of the sixteen joys. Thus.
"She has beautiful limbs" (varāṅgī) because she is endowed with all the praiseworthy qualities of youth, such as delicacy and so forth. ||3||

Having first performed the ritual procedures for the summoning of wisdom and so forth as before, the mantra-master, skilled in the ordinances, should meditate intensely on a single swastika revolving rapidly toward his own forehead. ||4||
He states another ritual action with the words "attraction of knowledge" (*jñānākarṣa*) and so forth. The practitioner (*mantrī*), who is the meditator (*bhāvaka*),
should visualize a *svastika* or a *nandyāvarta*.
"Suṣṭhu" means "well"; that from which there is happiness is the *svastika* (the auspicious cross), which is the *bindu*.
The instruction is that through the purification of that *bindu*, one should contemplate it as being turned back by union with the *caṇḍālī*.
And so it is said in the *Śabarapādīyasādhana*:

When a wise person sees the *nandyāvarta* near the *kolāsyā*, its meaning is as follows: it is called *nandī* because it causes joy (*nandayati*) together with the Goddess whose form is bliss; and because of its whirling motion (*āvarta*) arising from union with the *caṇḍālī*, it is the *nandyāvarta*.
"Whirling" means revolving without interruption, like a potter's wheel.
"Facing the *alika*" means facing the forehead (*alika*); it is so called because it possesses an *ala*—that is, a fang (*daṃṣṭrā*)—hence it is the head (*mastaka*). Facing that [head].
Alternatively, it is taught in the eighth chapter on secret signs (*chomā*) in the *Vajraḍāka*: "The animal (*paśu*) is the untruth."
Or, according to that intention,
it should be understood as "facing the false" (alikābhimukha) and "facing the face of the sacrificial animal" (paśumukhābhimukha).
"One" means precisely one.
"Swiftly" means due to the application of continuous rotation.
Having done what? He says: "One who knows the procedure," that is, one who knows the instruction. ||4||
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the previously described rotating wheel, red and blazing intensely, within a mountain cave on Mount Trikūṭa in the element of space. 5.
He states the specific duty to be performed with the words "tadanu" and so forth.
Immediately after that, one should meditate upon the wheel.
To the question of where it should be meditated upon, he says: "in the element possessing space."
"Viyat" means the sky, which is to say, empty or hollow; that which is joined with this is "viyadvat," namely the lotus of the Goddess. That which sustains is called a "dhātu."
The meaning of the sentence is that, due to its similarity with the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), it is "the interior of the lotus of the Goddess" therein.

Regarding "the cavern of the Trikūṭa mountain": it is *trikūṭa* because it is triangular, and it is a *giri* (mountain) because it is difficult to ascend and consists of precipices; [it is] in the cavern of that [mountain].
The meaning is: within [the heart], in the Supreme Source of Phenomena (dharmodayā) situated within the interior of the Goddess’s lotus.
Of what nature is the wheel? It is "revolving," as previously described.
The meaning is that it is exactly as if a crest-tip had been drawn with the falling of vermilion.
"Red" means crimson;
"blazing intensely" is because it consists of light.
It is "sad" (good) because it is joined with incomparable bliss. ||5||
That [wheel], though set in motion with extreme velocity, remained as steady as a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker;
it caused the great wheel of happiness to flow, performing a libation with a pouring stream of nectar.
He states the distinction: "That is steady," and so forth.
One should meditate upon that very wheel as if it were steady, as if motionless, due to the excessive speed—that is, the extreme movement—of the mind.

Herein is the instruction: from the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*) arising from the word "afterwards" in the subsequent verse, which serves as another verbal action, one should [meditate] after the visualization of the wheel upon the form of Caṇḍālī, blazing like a lamp in a windless place, like a motionless lamp.

One should understand that "one should see it shining intensely" is what is intended. Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the word "dīpta" (shining), which is a non-deviating qualifier— repeated in the phrase "like a lamp unshaken in a windless place"— the knowers of the tradition maintain that this entire, complete description by means of the neuter gender refers specifically to the Blessed Lady Caṇḍālī.
Otherwise, from the perspective of conventional reality (saṃvṛti), there would be no perception of Caṇḍālī at all,
because it has not been mentioned;
or else, this very wheel itself would be the form of Caṇḍālī.

Setting aside that interpretation which claims that both [the preceding and following verses] lack a traditional transmission (*asaṃpradāya*), it is said: what kind [of form]? It is the form of Caṇḍālī, which "melts" (*drāvayat*)—that is, causes to flow—the vast (*uru*) wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), bringing it to a state of liquefaction.
"Performing the ritual bath with a shower of flowing nectar" means performing the ablution by means of the flowing of nectar from the wheel of great bliss. (6)

One should subsequently behold, facing westward, that which has the nature of the three bodies, which is supreme, innate, and pervades the world, and which radiates an immeasurable succession of peaceful [forms]. //7//
"Having the nature of the three bodies" means having the essential form of the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies because they have become one unified whole. "Supreme" means...
Because it is of an uncommon nature (*asādhāraṇarūpatvāt*).
It is "supreme" (*paramam*) because it measures (*māti*) or delimits (*paricchinatti*) the innate moment (*sahajakṣaṇa*) which is most excellent.
It is "of the nature of the innate" (*sahajātmakam*).
Because its nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). It "pervades the world" because there exists nothing else distinct from it.
Alternatively, it is "pervading the universe" (*jagadvyāpin*) because it also has the nature of the universe itself.
Regarding the phrase "shimmering," and so forth:
Because it is that from which an immeasurable and uninterrupted stream of blissful happiness radiates, it is "thus" (*tathā*).
As for the term "facing backward" (*paścānmukha*):
The rule is that one should meditate upon the Goddess while facing westward.

Subsequently, the tradition (āmnāya) is as follows: one should meditate on the Goddess, who has the form of the syllable *vaṃ*, as she ascends from the *nirmāṇacakra* by means of a line in the form of *nāda* situated within the lunar drop (*bindu*), until she is endowed with all the aforementioned attributes.

That Blessed Lady, in the form of a line, having reached the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) at the opening of the three wheels (*cakras*), enters the *svastika* consisting of great bliss; then, having gone to the *mahāsukhacakra*, she [saturates] herself with a stream of nectar flowing incessantly—like clarified butter from a jar with a small hole melted by a mass of great flames.
The distinction is that while bathing [the deity], one should clearly rest in the inconceivable state (*acintyapada*).

In another interpretation, however, since the *caṇḍālī* was mentioned first, this should be understood as a qualification of the wheel (*cakra*) itself. One should first meditate upon the wheel as characterized by the aforementioned qualifications.
Afterwards, one should meditate on the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*); one should cause it to melt and perceive it.
However, the "wheel of great bliss" to be understood here is not that which is produced by the sprinkling of the essence of immeasurable radiance, because of the blazing of Caṇḍālī.
And because it is situated below that,

in that glorious *caṇḍālī-yoga*, which is the repository of all powers, there exists— just as in the case of sugarcane and the like where a divine juice arises through the power of pressing— a specific passion produced by the power of union, as found in the words of the Guru and other such teachings.
It is like the great light produced by the power inherent in wood and other materials for making a bed;
like the excellent offspring produced by the power of the mutual affection between husband and wife during sexual union;
and like the essence produced by the power of the falling stream in milk and other liquids.
It is like the special essence produced by the power of fire in butter,
like the fiery quality produced by the power of whirling in clay and similar substances,
and like the specific potency produced by medicinal power in grapes and the like.

Just as all desired objects arise in their entirety from the performance of mantras and other rites when the power of attraction has been generated, so too, through non-performance, everything is utterly destroyed and shattered for those following the Mahāyāna, just as it is for the Śrāvakas. And thus:
"By means of the union of the wheel and the lotus, the lotus is to be pressed."
And one should gradually churn it forth, having generated genuine affection.
Even upon the falling of the mountain's torrent, there arose from the void the power of the flame;
and from the flame, the power of the whirlpool, whose wife is the great passion-herb.
O Mahodaya, why should the power of attraction not arise from the vital breath?
It perishes along with its causes through the fault of non-performance.
Now, "purity" (*viśuddhi*) is so called because the Blessed Lady herself has presented herself for the sole purpose of delivering all sentient beings.
And thus, our Gurus have stated in the *Sādhanavibhaṅga* regarding the purity resulting from the application of vermilion:
"Although this face is pleased by the application of vermilion upon the mirror," [it is even more so here].
Nevertheless, in this context, the worship of the goddess in her internal form is superior.
Because it holds the indestructible wisdom (*vajra*), its lotus and its passion (*madana*) are also denoted by the term "Vajradhara";
having relied upon that [term] based on its sound, one should [visualize it] above.
Either place pure passion, like a serpent born from a purified state, within your most stainless mind as if in a mirror; or else, scatter the arising of all external and internal phenomena.
Write the seed-syllable of the mantra clearly with the beautiful *avadhūtī*, which— like a golden probe— is a mantra because it protects through contemplation.
Therein, the yogi should satisfy that [Goddess] who has arisen, who is stainless, whose form is perfectly pure gnosis,
and who has abandoned all disputes.
Her limbs are adorned with a garland of skulls because she wears a string of beads;
she is always united with the yoga of passion (rajas) by virtue of being composed of great bliss.
Alternatively, because he drinks the blood of the Māras, his mouth does not flow with blood;
in the ultimate sense, his root-face is that of a boar, while in the conventional sense, it is a human face.
This one has three eyes on her root-face due to the purity of seeing the three times;
this one has three eyes on her boar-face because she views both truths with equal vision.
The drop (bindu) situated with its face turned upward is called "risen above";
released by the whirling of the limbs, it becomes the cool-rayed moon through the purity of space.
Like the gait of one who has well-restrained and then released [a horse], due to the destruction of the remaining latent impressions (vāsanā),
the face of the Goddess— though slightly angry— is most excellent and auspicious because of her composure.

The right-hand [hand] holds a sharp-edged blade for the purpose of cutting through the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence; it is held in the right because its rays are sharp and piercing.
The skull-cup, filled with blood, represents the purity of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta);
it demonstrates union through perfectly pure passion.
Alternatively, [the skull] is the commitment of the essence of great bliss and constant compassion;
it is held in the left hand, filled with blood, flowing from the left side of the *bindu*.
Because it rises in the channel of space (khe), it is called the "space-staff" (khaṭvāṅga);
that very thing is called the "banner" (dhvaja) by virtue of being the sign of the yogi.
This fivefold Lord sports in the wheel of bliss;
when devoid of the five, the Bindu is Kālī, stationed at the head.
The Tathāgatas, made into bliss, are to be differentiated within the wheel of bliss;
thus the row of vajras shines, situated upon the head.
The *bindu* above, together with *saha*,
is capable of uprooting ignorance and the asuras;
because the *bindu* is of the nature of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), its face is that of a boar by way of convention.
The great bliss produced from that, pierced by the essence of great passion,
is likewise red— the root and the face— because it is the ultimate reality.
Even while looking at the sky with eyes closed, he did not see it as blood-red;
my final Guru said that because of its purity, the Goddess is red.
The form arisen from the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), the stable seed, the stainless—this very thing is called the "wheel" because it destroys the web of conceptual construction. ||7||
One should meditate upon this every day, at each junction of the day, or whenever there is leisure;
this is clearly stated to be practiced until the signs of accomplishment appear. ||8||
He states when one should meditate: "Every day," and so forth.
The connection is that one should meditate every day, that is, daily;
likewise at each junction (*sandhyā*), meaning during the four junctions of the day.
"According to the occasion" means according to the opportunity.
"Until the sign of accomplishment arises" means until that sign of accomplishment has not yet appeared.
This, however, is called the "manifest" (*vyakta*);
furthermore, this very manifest is said to be the sign (*nimitta*),
by which the yogi has produced the sign.
It is thus designated. ||8||
When joy arises effortlessly due to the absence of subsequent attachment,
this is clearly manifested;
there is no pain from being struck by a whip, a slap, or the like.
Then accomplishment will be not far off. ||9||
He states the sign: "arising without effort," and so forth.
The connection is that "then success will occur. "Not far off" means proximate.
To address the doubt as to "when," he says: "when it has been manifested, that is, made manifest.
Regarding the phrase "effortless" (*ayatnaja*), the meaning is that it is independent of effort because it flows by its own natural impulse (*svarasavāhitayā*).
To the question "From what would that arise?", he says: "Joy" is great bliss; its "impulse" is its momentum;
its "continuity" is its non-abandonment; [the result arises] from that.
To the question "When and what would not arise?", he says: "Who," and so forth.
A whip is a leather thong;
a slap is a blow with the palm.
By the word "etcetera," one includes kicks with the feet and so forth.
Even when struck by these, no sensation arises;
that indeed is the meaning of "attainment" (siddhi). ||9||
If the sharp sound of beaten drums and other instruments does not fall within the range of hearing,
then unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment is attained.
For one who meditates, there is the attainment of great powers in dreams before long. ||10||

He states the second sign with the words "of those who have been struck," and so forth. The connection is that at that time, awakening (*bodha*) is attained (*ādhiyate*), meaning it is reached (*prāpyate*).
"Anuttarā" means that of which no superior or more excellent [state] exists.
"Agryā" means the foremost.
It is of the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) because it exists above all else.
To address the doubt as to "when [this occurs]," he says: "of those beaten," and so forth.

Even in the case of mṛdaṅgas and other instruments that have been beaten to the highest degree, the sharp and excellent sound is not experienced by the sense organ within the range of hearing—that is, within the domain of the auditory faculty; this is the remainder of the sentence.
Regarding the word "svapna" (in a dream):
the particle "api" (even) is to be understood here.
Even in a dream—that is, even during sleep—for one who possesses meditation, the practitioner of yoga, supreme accomplishment shall occur before long.
The meaning is that even while asleep, the yogi remains absorbed in the samādhi of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and acts as the captivator of Vajravilāsinī.
Alternatively, the sense is that if one perceives such a sign even in a dream, accomplishment (*siddhi*) will indeed occur. ||10||
Having perceived the signs of accomplishment in a cemetery, a mountain thicket, at the foot of a tree, or similar locations,
the wise practitioner, dwelling there, should constantly practice the yoga of the utpannakrama.
He states the specific location with the words "having seen," and so forth.
*Sudhīḥ* means a wise person, a scholar, or one possessed of discernment (*saprajña*).
The connection is that he should perform—that is, practice—the yoga of the internal self (*adhyātmayoga*), which is the yoga of the arisen stage (*utpannakrama*).
Having done what? He says: "having seen the sign of accomplishment" (*siddhinimitta*).
That is, having recognized this aforementioned sign of accomplishment.
"Dwelling" (*nivasan*)—that is to say:
Remaining in meditative absorption (samāhita), where? He says: "in the cemetery" (pitṛvana), and so forth. A cemetery (pitṛvana) is a charnel ground (śmaśāna).
The rest is indeed easy to understand.
However, according to the alternative interpretation, the "forest" of the father Vajradhara is "great bliss" (mahāsukha) because it is secluded and because it is a forest of passion (rāga).
Since the word *pitṛvana* is a synonym for *śmaśāna* (the cemetery),
or because it is characterized by the cessation of the eight consciousnesses,
the meaning is "abiding therein."

[it is also] at the base of trees and so forth.
[The roots] *kṛṣū* and *vṛṣū* mean "to sprinkle."
It is called a "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) because it holds the *bodhicitta* which is being poured forth; or it is the "vajra," namely the *avadhūtī*.
The meaning is that one dwells at its root, offering up the mind.

"Unceasingly" means as it occurs without interruption. ||11||
Upon the accomplishment [of this], the earth and the other elements indeed undergo dissolution in successive order, one after another;
then there arises that which is like the sky, luminous, consisting of pure gnosis, and real. (12)
He describes the majesty of that moment with the words beginning "In the accomplishment" (*siddhau*).
Upon the accomplishment of this yoga, there occurs the dissolution (*laya*) of the earth and the other great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as the earth and so forth,
in successive order, one after another.
The meaning is that each subsequent element dissolves into the one preceding it. And so it is said:
"The earth-element dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire.
The underlying intention, however, is as follows:
Releasing the solidity of earth, the moisture of the water element, the heat of fire,
and the motion of wind, he sinks into the ocean of consciousness.
And so it is said in the Hevajra:
"Earth, water, wind, fire, and space itself—
all these do not obstruct the experience of the self-awareness of oneself and others in an instant."

Alternatively, the elements beginning with earth, which flow through the left and right channels and possess the nature of mandalas— such that the earth-maṇḍala enters the water-maṇḍala and so forth in succession until they enter the wisdom-maṇḍala, whose essential nature is imperishable bliss—
as it is stated in the *Kālacakra*:

Earth dissolves into water, and water likewise into fire; fire into wind, and wind into space; and space indeed proceeds into the tenfold causal sign, and the causal sign into the Jñānakāya—the unstruck, supreme bliss, imperishable, and possessing all aspects.
O Lord of Men, through knowledge, supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), and accomplishment (*siddhi*) arise for men in this very life.
To the question, "How then does the yogin manifest at that time? he says: "Then it shines like the sky.
It shines resembling the sky.

Like dream-cognition, it is independent of an object of knowledge and is mere self-luminosity;
"Being" (sat) is its undifferentiated form. ||12||
One should recognize them by their signs; those who know that [reality] understand the signs to be fivefold.
Therefore, a yogi who is concentrated should perceive them with the mind. (13)
He states the cause for knowing [it]: "One should know," and so forth.
The connection is that one should know that knowledge by means of the signs (cihna) which are about to be described. As for the signs:

Furthermore, the signs (*cihnāni*) and marks (*nimittāni*) are fivefold, consisting of five types; those who know them—namely, those who possess the knowledge born of yoga regarding that non-duality (*tadadvaita-yoga*)—know them, for it is only for them that those signs arise.
"For this very reason" means precisely because of this mode of being.
Or rather, from the very samādhi of emptiness,
the yogi who is skilled in reality should perceive those [signs],
being thus composed in meditation.
"With undistracted mind" means: by means of the mind of the supreme dhyāna alone, because it is not an object for other consciousnesses. ||13||
First, there is the appearance of a mirage; the second sign has the form of smoke;
the third is like fireflies; and the fourth is clearly radiant like a lamp. (14)
He asks, "What are those signs? and replies with the words beginning "First," and so forth.
A sign resembling a mirage—that is, like a shimmering heat-haze—arises first.
Even though this is so, nevertheless, according to the oral instruction, it should be understood that the very first sign is indeed in the form of smoke.
The mirage is the second. First, the yogi whose mind is fixed on space sees smoke, and subsequently the mirage and so forth.
As it is said in the *Kālacakra*:
With minds unattached to space, with unblinking eyes, having entered the vajra-path, from emptiness there appear smoke, a mirage, a manifest and stainless firefly,
and a lamp; then flame, the moon, the sun, and the vajras, and finally the supreme digit and the drop are seen.
In the midst of that is the reflection of gnosis, the manifold saṃbhogakāya devoid of objects.

And therein, through the instruction of the guru regarding the six limbs, the yogi first perceives smoke in space and not a mirage; this should be known from one's own experience, followed by the mirage.
Subsequently, the smoke and so forth appear free from conceptual construction, like a reflected image (*pratisenā*).
As it is said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"For that [vision], having omniscience as its cause, functions when one is near to the attainment of siddhi;
subsequently, it has a form like an illusion and a form like a dream, moment by moment.
Or else, "it is like a mirage."
The entire world is false for the yogin, like a mirage;
this is the meaning of "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*).
This is because it appears through the apprehension of something as being what it is not.
"Having the form of smoke" means that knowledge of space arises precisely in the form of smoke,
as well as [the vision of] illusory elephants and so forth.
The meaning is that one perceives the entire universe— which is dependently originated, devoid of intrinsic nature, and a mere appearance— as having the form of smoke, like an illusory elephant.
"Like a firefly" means just as a firefly flashes momentarily in the sky, in the space.
Likewise, the third sign is that the light of gnosis takes emptiness as its object in both a manifest and unmanifest manner.
Regarding "the fourth":
the fourth sign is blazing like a lamp.
Alternatively, it is like a lamp: brilliant, clear, and manifest;
though it remains for a long time in the form of light, it is perishable once deprived of the awakening.
The sense is that this occurs through association with unwholesome friends (akalyāṇamitra). ||14||
The fifth sign is luminous and non-conceptual, resembling a cloudless sky;
having thus attained this sign, one obtains the great mudrā. ||15||
He states the fifth characteristic, beginning with "free from clouds" and so forth:
"resembling the sky at midday in the stainless autumn,
luminous."
Because its nature is that of knowledge (*jñāna*).
"Non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*) means that the fifth sign, which is free from duality, arises.
"Thus" (*evam*) [means as follows].
Thus, the yogin who has attained the signs of knowledge arising in this sequence "receives"—that is, grasps—joy and bliss; hence she is called *mudrā*.
He "attains," meaning he realizes, the *mahatīm* (great) one, i.e., the *mahāmudrā*;
the meaning is that he becomes a possessor of the *mahāmudrā*. ||15||
Desiring to rise, having prostrated to the Yoginī and the Lord, and having uttered the syllable *mūḥ*,
one who possesses the wisdom of reality should rise and perform his duty.
The knower of yoga should always remain joined in union with yoga. 16.
Thus concludes the rule for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of attaining the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
He states another duty with the words "desirous of rising," and so forth.
The connection is that the yogi, desiring to rise, should perform his task after having risen.
To the question "Having done what?", he says: "having prostrated before the Yoginī."
Having paid homage to the Goddess,
and likewise to the Lord—
the Lord as well as the Guru.
"Wood! [This refers to] that which is situated on the head.
"Uttering the syllable *mūḥ*."
The meaning is that having uttered the *mūḥ*-syllable, the mantra of dismissal, one should perform the ritual activity immediately after the dismissal.
Regarding how the practitioner (*bhāvaka*) remains while performing that activity, he says: "He should remain," and so forth;
he should always remain and dwell by means of the pair of yogas, that is, through the union with the two mudrās.
The meaning is that one should meditate upon the goddess *Sacakrā* and *Caṇḍālī*.
Alternatively, it should be understood that by way of the arrangement of cause and effect, the two *caṇḍālīs* themselves constitute the two yogas.

As for those who first see the syllable *vaṃ*, surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka* and so forth, in a blazing form within the secondary *dharmodaya*-cakra situated inside the *bhagavatī-dharmodaya*-cakra, and subsequently [visualize] a line of rays from the syllable *vaṃ* as subtle as a lotus fiber—

The commentators explain that, having pierced through the three wheels consisting of the nature of the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*), the dharma wheel (*dharmacakra*), and the enjoyment wheel (*sambhogacakra*), one follows the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) and, by means of the door of the cool-rayed moon which has been flooded [with light], brings great bliss to manifestation; thus the object of yoga should be practiced. However, in their view, because the term *yogayuga* is incorrectly explained as "attachment to yoga," only a single yoga is established.
And this [system] was not accepted by our teachers because it is not mentioned in the traditional scriptures and because it contradicts the *Sādhana* of Śabarapāda;
yet, some practitioners are seen even among those who follow his view.
"Yogavid" means one who knows yoga.
"Tattvadhī" means one whose intellect (dhī), that is, wisdom (prajñā), has the true reality (tattva) as its object; such is the meaning. ||16||
Thus ends the procedure for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-vidhi*) in the *Marmakalikā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna-saṃsiddhi*).
[Now, the procedure for favoring disciples:
Having been repeatedly entreated by the disciples who have formed a maṇḍala and bowed at his lotus feet,
the mantra-master should bestow his favor upon them on the tenth lunar day.
He states the procedure for favoring the disciples, beginning with "being requested" and so forth.
The connection is that the mantra-master, the guru, should perform the favoring of those disciples.
And "being requested" means:
Being requested many times by his disciples, he indeed performed it; "by those who have prepared the maṇḍala" means this.
"By those who have performed the guru-maṇḍala," means by those prostrating at the lotus-feet, i.e., fallen at the lotus-feet. "On the lunar day of the tenth" (tithau daśamyām).

Because other [days] than the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇā) are not accepted as the days of the observance (samaya-tithi), and because the Yoginīs consist of the nature of non-perception, they have authority only in the dark fortnight. ||1||

Having worshipped the Goddess in the form of the mantra residing within the wheel, and having performed the yoga, one who has recited the mantra should take the supreme primordial [substance] and emerge from there. ||2||
He states another duty of the Guru with the words "having worshipped," and so forth.
The connection is that "the practitioner of mantra should depart. The word "from there" refers to the place where the Goddess was worshipped.
Having done what? He says: "having fully worshipped" (saṃpūjya). That is, having honored the Goddess.
"In the form of the mantra" (mantrarūpām) means [the Goddess] who exists in the form of the mantra as established in the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra).
"Residing in the wheel" means residing in the triangle drawn on the surface of a mirror smeared with vermilion. And thus:
"In the center of a three-petaled lotus, upon a mirror grey with powdered vermilion..."
The Guru, having also worshipped the image composed of mantra that has been painted, should depart.
Thus our teachers [state] in the *Sādhanavibhaṅga*:
"the yoga that has been prescribed."
Having formed an attachment to external and internal wisdom,
his mental heroism is first stimulated by the drinking of a little intoxicant; then, having cast away the multitude of conceptual constructions, emptiness is made to shine forth.
Then, having performed yoga, one attains supreme bliss through union with wisdom; such is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*).
"Having taken" (*ādāya*) means having grasped.
"The supreme primordial vessel" refers to the cup accompanied by *madana*.
"Chanted with mantra" means empowered by the three syllables.
The meaning is that, for the sake of pleasing the disciple, he himself should take the vessel and go out. ||2||

Then the Guru should look upon the disciple—who has performed the five circumambulations, stands with palms joined above his head, has offered the ritual fee, and wears a garland of flowers—while the disciple meditates on the Sole Lord (Ekanātha). ||3||
He states another duty of the Guru with the words "atha" and so forth.
The connection is: "Then, immediately thereafter, the Guru should look at the disciple.
"Having performed the five mandalas while standing upright" means as follows.
It should be understood that he is situated at the head of the mandala within the five mandalas that have been prescribed; this is to be known from the instruction "standing above" (ūrdhvasthita),
or alternatively, by the grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) of the term "standing above."
And in that system, there is the instruction that [the deity] stands in the center of the mandala.
The tradition (āmnāya) holds that the fivefold mandala should be constructed with cow dung and so forth, even without [the recitation of] the mantra.
Furthermore, some maintain the lineage tradition that one should gaze upon the disciple who has been established within the mandala of the five Tathāgatas.
"Having given the sacrificial fee (*dattadakṣiṇam*)" means:
I desire the surrender of wealth, gold, male and female slaves, and my own body.
"Bearing a garland of flowers" means: [he is] wearing a flower wreath.
Holding a garland of flowers with both hands slightly opened and joined together— thus one should meditate upon the Lord.
"Who indeed has meditated upon whom on his head? He is the Lord, the Guru.
The intended meaning is that [the disciple] should look [at the Guru] in order to produce a state of spiritual possession (āveśa). ||3||
Thereafter, having meditated upon the aforementioned wheel of goddesses, with its radiating rays and swift motion, the wielder of the vajra should bestow it upon the body of the disciple. ||4||
He states the subsequent duty with the words "tadanu ca" and so forth.

"Tadanu" means immediately after the visualization; the connection is that the guru should give—that is, present—to that disciple, who "bears the vajra" (vajrabhṛt), the vessel of passion (madanapātra).
Regarding the word "dhyātvā" (having meditated):
Having reflected:
as it has been stated, the "circle of goddesses" (devīcakra) is the triangular wheel (trikoṇacakra) described at the time of the application of vermilion (sindūra);
and "emerging rays" means radiating beams of light.
"Like a flame" means whirling with speed.
"In the body of the resident" means in the body of the disciple.
It should be understood from the instruction that [the location] is in the *dharmodayā* below the navel.
Regarding the reading *antevāsī*, since it would consist of thirteen *mātrās* and thus result in a metrical break (*chandobhaṅga*), one should not accept an unexpressed compound (*anukta-samāsa*).
Some do not write this [verse], stating that the meaning of this *gāthā* is to be understood from the instruction.
The instruction on the wheel is written as follows:

First, one should fashion a triangle three finger-breadths wide and radiant, preceded by red flowers and drawn with the ring finger, containing the syllables *sūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *kṣaṃ*. This is the wheel of the *ava* [vowels] and so forth; the wise one should construct it thus.
Upon the application of vermilion, one should draw a three-petaled lotus filled with the mantra consisting of five syllables, together with the seed-syllable *vaṃ* at its center;
and in the cardinal directions, one should draw four svastikas.
Even in the *Śrīvajradevīkamala*, which deals with desired [attainments], there is a wheel of mantras situated within the *dharmodayā*.
As it was stated there: "That triangle also should revolve as a wheel."
And the best among those who possess knowledge.
And in the rite of possession for the disciple, the lotus below the navel should be meditated upon as the true Guru;
that which is filled with mantra is likewise a triangle, yet it is traditionally taught to be a hexagon.
On the cloth, one should draw a three-petalled lotus where the Goddess herself is alone;
or else, it is seen that this pair [of lotuses] is adorned by a group of six deities or a hexagon.
Furthermore, at the time of preparing the maṇḍala on the ground, the virtuous ones should extract the power of the six-cornered mantra;
all six goddesses are to be worshipped here in the corners starting from the east, as well as the svastika-maṇḍala.

Thus there may be his possession (āveśa), [characterized by] longing, trembling, tears, falling down, the arising of knowledge, and even identity with one's own nature, according to the sequence. ||5||
He states the characteristics of possession (*āveśa*) with the words "in this way," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "In this manner, through this sequence, there shall be possession—that is, the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by the deity—of that disciple."
He states the characteristics of possession (āveśa) with the words beginning "thrill" (utkalikā), etc.
"Thrill" (utkalikā) refers to horripilation;
"trembling" (prakampana) refers to intense shaking.
"Bāṣpa" means a flickering descent;
"pāta" means falling.
"Jñānotpāda" is the attainment of knowledge of the past, future, and present.

The sense is that he tells everything. Regarding "and similarity" (*sārūpyam*): the meaning is that for the disciple who has been possessed by this sequence, there arises not only possession (*āveśa*), but also the thorough knowledge of his own true nature (*svarūpa*).
For without the thorough knowledge of one's own true nature, it is impossible to bestow grace upon disciples. ||5||

Thereafter, one should explain the meditative absorption (samādhi) and the worship mantra of Vajrayoginī to one who possesses faith, is endowed with virtue, and has true devotion that does not distinguish between the Guru and the Buddha. (6)
He states the unsurpassed rite with the words "tadanu" and so forth. The connection is that immediately after the disciple’s inquiry, the Guru should explain the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
And regarding the mantra for the worship of Vajrayoginī:
one should also state the mantra prescribed for the purpose of worshipping Kiravaktrā.
"For one endowed with faith" means...
For one who has developed firm conviction regarding the truths, the Three Jewels, karma, its results, and so forth, [there arises the thought]:
"The Buddha exists; the Dharma exists;
the Sangha exists."
The meaning is that this refers to one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is permeated by specific latent impressions (vāsanā) such as "evil exists" or "merit exists.
Regarding the term *guṇinaḥ*: [it means] "of one possessing qualities."
"Endowed with all virtues;
through true devotion inseparable from the Guru and the Buddha. Here, "Guru and Buddha" refers to the Guru and the Buddha [taken together].
He whose correct devotion toward those two is undivided is "one such as that.
And so it has been said: "The Guru is the Buddha, the Guru is the Dharma, and likewise the Guru is the Saṅgha."
For this very reason, he is called "the one whose lap is the Lord" (*nāthāṅkaka*), because it is the Guru alone who is taken as the place of Vairocana. ||6||
One should not explain this yoga—which produces immediate conviction and is well-established—to a disciple whose mind is devoid of faith or who is lacking in devotion. ||7||
He states the prohibition: "One should not tell, nor should one reveal, this yoga to a disciple.
To the question "To what kind of person? he replies: "To one whose mind is devoid of faith," that is, to one whose heart has abandoned faith.
"Of one devoid of devotion" means of one who lacks devotion toward the Guru and the Buddhas.
"Producing immediate conviction" means...
It produces immediate understanding.
In the reading *saṃpratyayakaram*, there is an excess of a *mātrā* and a violation of the sixth *gaṇa*.
Regarding *susiddhaṃ vā*: it means either "possessing excellent accomplishment" (*suṣṭhu siddhimantam*) or "well-perfected" (*suniṣpannam*).
The reading "susiddhidam" is also a corruption,
because it would entail the same faults mentioned previously. ||7||
But for him who performs worship of the circle of goddesses conjoined with the mantra, the eight fears and great sins depart. (8)
He states the benefit: "he brings about," and so forth.
The connection is that the fears of that yogin depart, meaning they perish.
"Eight" refers to those produced by lions, elephants, fire, and so on.
"Sins" refers to the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) and so forth. "Great" means formidable terrors.
He states the cause for their pacification with the words beginning with "he performs," and so on.
The meaning is: for that yogi who performs the worship of the wheel of the goddesses, the six-spoked wheel of the Blessed Lady;
[the phrase] "endowed with mantra" refers to this.
For one who has performed worship with the mantra of the Goddess and the mantras of the six Yoginīs, or else with the previously mentioned sindūra-mantra within a complete triangle; ||8||
Misfortune, poverty, disease, old age, suffering, and dejection;
wandering, strife, impurity, and afflictions, as well as various kinds of pain. (9)
He states another benefit, beginning with "durbhagatā" and so forth:
"durbhagatā" is misfortune or lack of good fortune in the worlds;
"dāridrya" is poverty or being destitute.
Disease refers to painful ailments and the like; old age is senility;
suffering is the affliction of body and mind.
Mental distress is the suffering of the mind.
Delusion is error, such as the perception of what is non-dharma as dharma—
for example, the view of non-Buddhists that violence leads to heaven.
*Kali* means dispute. *Kaluṣa* means sin, or the impurity taught through the greatness of the Kali age. *Kleśas* are passion, hatred, and delusion.
"Pain" refers to various kinds [of suffering], and "various types of calamities" refers to disturbances caused by various kinds of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction.
The word *api* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed).
It is connected with the previously mentioned verse by the phrase "they depart" (*apayānti*). ||9||
He who recites the Cakra-mantra while meditating upon it in his heart with speech restrained attains the eight siddhis, as well as the five superknowledges and the eight qualities. ||10||
He states another benefit: "He who recites," and so forth.

The connection is that he attains the eight accomplishments (*siddhi*), such as the eye-salve (*añjana*) and the pill (*guṭikā*). Regarding the "five superknowledges" (*pañcābhijñā*): [they are] the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), [the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows].
divine hearing, knowledge of the minds of others, and the power of traveling through space;
And the recollection of former abodes;
likewise, the eight qualities,
namely the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth.
Or [the powers] beginning with *aṇiman*.
"He who," and so forth:
he who, having meditated upon the mantra together with the discus and having placed it within the heart—that is, the mind—[attains success].
"He mutters"—the meaning is that this would indeed happen for him.
"And by means of speech-restraint" refers to the restraint of speech through the practice of silence (*nirodhavāk*). ||10||
He who meditates with effort every day at the four junctions of the day upon her whose face is radiant as the sun conquers death, which cannot be overcome even by Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha. (11)
He states another benefit, beginning with "dhyāyati" (he meditates):
"Whoever meditates upon Kiravaktrā, the boar-faced one—that is, brings her onto the mind through intense yoga—he conquers death; such is the connection."
He describes what kind of death it is with the words "Hari-hara," etc.;
the meaning is that it is "unconquered" (aparājitām), meaning it cannot be overcome even by Keśava and the others.
"Every day" (pratidivasam) means constantly.
"With effort" means preceded by worship and other such acts;
"at the four junctions" refers to dawn, midday, evening, and midnight. (11)
For him, there arise garments, food, drink, wealth, grain, vast lands, palaces, divine beds, seats, and means of accomplishment,
as well as various beloved sciences.
He who meditates upon her whose face is like a flash of lightning, accompanied by a wheel. ||12||
Thus concludes the procedure for the grace bestowed upon disciples, together with its benefits, for the sake of the perfect attainment of the knowledge of reality.
He states another benefit: "clothing, food," and so forth.
The connection is that for one who meditates on Aśanikolamukhī, that is, Vajrakolāsyā, clothing and other such things arise—that is, they are obtained.
"Together with the wheel" (sacakrām).
Together with the wheel filled with the mantra in the center of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya);
the garment is Chinese silk;
the food consists of edibles and so forth.
Beverages refer to drinks and the like; wealth refers to gems and the like;
grain refers to barley, wheat, and so forth.
The vast land is the exceedingly expansive earth;
the palace is a delightful mansion;
and the divine bed is a mattress of variegated cloth inlaid with diverse jewels.
The seat refers to the lion-throne and so forth;
the means of accomplishment refers to elephants, horses, and the like;
and "beloved ones" refers to young women who are dear to the heart.
"Various" means they are skilled in many kinds of amorous songs and instrumental music.
"Divine" means they are desirable even to the gods. (12)
Thus ends the procedure for favoring the disciples in the *Marmakalikā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the attainment of the knowledge of reality.
[Now, the procedure for extracting the mantra:
Hereafter, I shall explain the extraction of the mantra that is the heart of Vajrayoginī, which has been transmitted from ear to ear and from mouth to mouth in succession. (1)
"Regarding 'the extraction of the mantra' and so forth:
the connection is that he will explain the extraction of the mantra.
'Beyond this' [means] as follows."
"Immediately after the possession and so forth, the supreme or most excellent [mantra] is the Heart of Vajrayoginī. This means that the "Heart" of Kolamukhī is the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra).
Like a heart, it is the heart;
"from ear to ear" means by word of mouth;
"arrived" means come together.
The sense is that it is because [this teaching] is of an extremely secret nature. "From mouth to mouth" means from the mouth of one guru to the mouth of another guru.
"So be it.
The sense is that, because its activity is unerring, it is like one lamp [producing] another lamp.
"Successively" means by way of a sequence. ||1||
Having drawn a circle as previously described, provided with the abode of the hosts of Maruts,
one should there, following the sequence, write the *āli* and likewise the *kāli*, minus one.
The Wheel says: "As previously stated," and so forth.
*Āli* refers to the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*.
Likewise, by that same sequence, *kāli* refers to the thirty-three consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*.
The connection is with the word "should write. Regarding the phrase "minus one":
this means excluding the letter *kṣa*, because that [letter] has already been expressed by the letters *ṣa* and *ka*.
Having done what? He says: "having drawn the wheel as previously described.
The meaning is: having drawn the wheel in the form of the *dharmodayā* as previously described, one should write [the mantra] there in the center.
The word "as" (*iva*), however, is for the purpose of indicating merely the form of the *dharmodayā*.
Because the previously mentioned wheel is inscribed with the mantra of the Goddess; "endowed with the abode of the hosts of Maruts" means it is endowed with— that is,
has reached— an abode or location corresponding in number to the forty-nine winds that constitute the hosts of Maruts.
The meaning is that even the forty-nine squares have the form of the *dharmodayā*.
And it is said in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*: "The entire universe is the *dharmodayā*."
"Successively" means in order.
The sequence of the wheels as it has come down through oral instruction is written here:
moon, fire, arrows, sages, nine, Śaṅkara, and Madana, according to the sequence of the compartments.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of those [deities] having the form of the *dharmodayā* according to the oral instruction.
Having drawn the *dharmodayā* before one, which consists of three lines,
in such a way that each of the three lines has six sections, so too in the middle.

Thus, having drawn seven houses multiplied by seven in a clockwise direction, the letter *a* falls upon the central square (*varaṭaka*), and that [letter] in the middle is *ha*. Through the purification of the three qualities, there is a three-petalled lotus; within it, the letters are dissolved into the *dharmodayās* through the very purification of the wind.
Everything is thus condensed as "pavana.
The Goddess, whose form is the letter A, is situated within the filaments;
the Lord Heruka, whose form is the letter Ha, resides in the central region. (2)

Having first written the triad consisting of the letter *ja* with *ra* below, the letter *ḍa* with *ra* below, and adorned by the letter *ha* with *ra* below— these three joined together form the six-syllable mantra that illuminates the ultimate reality.
He states the extraction of the mantra: "jhādharaga," and so forth.
The connection is that the triad should be written at the beginning.
[The term] *avyaktaguṇasaṃdohe* is in the neuter gender.
He asks, "What is that? and replies: "jhādharagaṃ" means situated below the letter jha;
that is, the letter 'a' which stands beneath jha. This is the meaning.
The letter *u* is situated below the letter *ḍa*.
"Adorned by that which is below *ha*" means it is marked on its head by the letter *ma*, which is below *ha*.
"Joined together" [refers to this].
From the letters *a* and *u*, the letter *o* arises;
in place of the letter *m*, there is a *bindu*.
This should be understood according to the instruction that it is "together with the nasal" (*sendu*).
The meaning is that first this very triad, which is the nature of the syllable *oṃ*, should be written:
*oṃ oṃ oṃ*.
It is called "the six-syllabled" because it conveys a specific intended meaning.

The traditional meaning of the word *oṃ* is that through the very union of the drops (*bindu*), the syllable *u*, which has the nature of wind, dissolves into emptiness, which has the form of the syllable *a*. As for the triad, it is for the purpose of establishing unity in the form of body, speech, and mind.
Therefore, "illuminating reality" (tattvaparidīpi) means that which reveals reality. ||3||
The letter *bha* joined with the one situated above, and the one situated above joined with *cha*; thereafter, the one situated above *ṭa* should be written.
Then, the one below *ḍa* joined with the one below *ṣa*, and the one below *ṣa* joined with the one situated above *śa*. (4)
Another says: "The upward-moving from *bha*, and so forth.
