Accompanied by the lower *ḍa* and the void (*śūnya*), situated above the three folds and resting on the jewel-plane;
joined with the lower *tha*, situated below the *śa*, and also conjoined with that which is below the *ña*. ||9||
He speaks again: "Accompanied by the lower part of *ḍa* and the void," and so forth.
The lower part of the letter *ḍa* is *u*, and the void is the nasal drop (*bindu*).
The instruction is that it is accompanied by the *indu* (the nasal bindu).

Together with those two, there is a triad; furthermore, from the letter *va*, there is the letter *ha* situated below it (*talaga*). Thus, "three times below" means three *ha*s situated below, together with three short *u*s—meaning three *ha*s accompanied by three short *u*s:
*huṃ huṃ huṃ*.

Although three *hūṃ* syllables are accepted in the ritual procedure (*sādhanaprakriyā*) of the venerable Śabara, nevertheless, because this is a distinct ritual procedure, the acceptance of the short [syllable] here is likewise beyond dispute.
"Situated above" means that the letter *pha* is positioned above the letter *ca*.
"The base of *ra*" means that the letter *ṭa* is the base of the letter *ra*.
This also applies to the extraction of the syllable *phaṭ*.
The three *phaṭ* syllables are to be understood from the oral instruction:
"joined with the lower part of *tha*, situated at the lower part of *śa*, and also joined with the lower part of *ña*.
The letter situated below *tha* is *va*.
That which is joined with that [the letter *śa*] and situated below the letter *śa* is the letter *sa*.
It is conjoined with the vowel *a* situated below the letter *ña*; thus it is "svā. 9.
This secret mantra of the goddess Aśanī, composed of the syllables "sa-ya-ma-dhya-gaṃ jha-vā-ma-ga-sa," should be written, recited, and meditated upon. 10.
He spoke again: "That which is situated between *sa* and *ya*, joined with the leftward-moving *jha*. This means that the letter *ha* is situated between the letters *sa* and *ya*.
It is joined—that is, conjoined—with the letter *ā*, which moves to the left of *jha*. Thus: *hā*.
"The secret is formed by the aforementioned syllables."
This secret, which is not to be disclosed, has been composed, extracted, and drawn forth from the aforementioned vowels and consonants;
for it is the cause of attaining the supreme state.
To the question "Who is this?", he says: "This mantra belongs to the goddess Aśanidevī. Aśanidevī is Vajradevī, also known as Kolāsyā.
This is its mantra.
Of what nature is it? It is to be written, recited, and meditated upon.
"To be written" refers to [its use] in the ritual procedures for applying vermilion and so forth.
The mantra is to be recited, which brings joy born from the fatigue of meditative cultivation;
it is to be visualized within the lotus-womb of the Goddess.
The particle "tu" (but/and) is for the purpose of indicating a specific characteristic. ||10||
The wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial tree, the excellent vase, and even the glorious cow of plenty are praised;
yet when they are being sought after, they bestow wealth here—
But justice bestows happiness along with wealth. ||11||
Thus ends the procedure for extracting the mantra for the sake of attaining the knowledge of reality.
He states the benefits, beginning with "the wish-fulfilling gem" (*cintāmaṇi*), and so forth.
The connection is as follows: this king of mantras bestows wealth, happiness, and unsurpassed bliss.
The "wish-fulfilling gem" (*cintāmaṇi*) is a particular kind of jewel that rains down riches.
The wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpakuṭha*) is the *kalpavṛkṣa*;
the foremost jar (*agrakumbha*) is the auspicious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*);
and *śrī* is prosperity (*sampatti*).
*Kāma* means longing;
the cow that impels it is *Śrī-Kāmadhenu*—this is the meaning. "Those being accomplished" refers to them.
All four of those, when practiced, bestow or grant worldly wealth and riches in this cycle of existence;
however, this [practice] grants both enjoyment and liberation—this is the meaning. ||11||
Thus ends the procedure for the extraction of mantras in the *Marmakalikā-nāma-tattvajñānasaṃsiddhipañjikā*.
The ritual procedure for worship—the method of worship transmitted through tradition—is now written down.
First, having taken recourse to the divine ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), [one recites]: *oṃ sumbha niśumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the four-faced mantras: *oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, *oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*,

*oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, one should consecrate the ground in a clean place with the three-syllable mantra (*tryakṣara*), using fragrant substances possessing color and essence, such as saffron, red sandalwood, and the like.

*Oṃ āṃ gāṃ rāṃ ḍeṃ māṃ kāṃ preṃ triṃ kāṃ kaṃ raṃ kaṃ hiṃ praṃ guṃ soṃ luṃ maṃ kuṃ.* Having first recited each one of these previously mentioned four-faced mantras, one should cause a square mandala to be drawn with the left hand, starting from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise (*vāmāvarta*).

One should also perform the recitation of the twenty-four syllables of the seats (*pīṭha*), sub-seats (*upapīṭha*), fields (*kṣetra*), sub-fields (*upakṣetra*), meeting-places (*chandoha*), sub-meeting-places (*upacchandoha*), confluences (*melāpaka*), sub-confluences (*upamelāpaka*), cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*), and sub-cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*), beginning with *pūṃ*, *jāṃ*, and so forth.

Then, having drawn a six-pointed mandala upon the tip of the ring finger of the left hand with a syllable *vaṃ* shining in its center, and having drawn four svastikas outside it in the sequence of the directions starting from the east, one should trace the line with: *oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ svāhā*.

One should then consecrate the line with: *oṃ surekhe sarvatathāgatādhitiṣṭhantu svāhā*. Then, with the feet planted and the gaze directed upward, one should form the flame-mudrā (*jvālāmudrā*) by sounding the syllable *pheṃ* from the head and whirl it in a counter-clockwise direction.
Preceded by the mantras for summoning and so forth, such as *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, one should summon the Goddess residing in the Akaniṣṭha realm, cause her to enter, bind her, and satisfy her.

Then, one should visualize that very Goddess, surrounded by the six Yoginīs, red in color, endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments (*rasa*) beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), accompanied by the lords of the eight directions, and together with various yogas, Yoginīs, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, ḍākas, and ḍākinīs, forming a perfectly pure maṇḍala of the samaya.

Having visualized her dancing in the midst of this cremation ground through meditative cultivation, one should worship the Goddess with red-colored flowers using the heart-mantra arising from the extraction of the mantra.

Then, one should worship the six goddesses in the six corners with the mantras *oṃ vaṃ hoṃ yoṃ hrīṃ moṃ heṃ hrīṃ hraṃ hraṃ phaṭ*, which are combined with the three-syllable mantra and interspersed with the foot-epithets for addressing the six goddesses.
Furthermore, one should worship the *nandyāvarta* designs in the four directions with the mantra *oṃ āḥ nandyāvarta hūṃ phaṭ*.
According to another tradition, one should also worship the four goddesses, beginning with Ḍākinī, in the center and in the directions starting from the east.
Then, having performed the praise, worship, and so forth, one should dismiss [the deities] with the syllable *mur*.
According to one's capacity, the worship of the maiden (*kumārī*) should be performed with garments, food, drink, flour-cakes, and other offerings.
She is to be brought under control and made obedient.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for worship.
The Ritual of the Bali Offering:
The ritual of the bali offering is now described.

First, having placed before oneself a lotus vessel and so forth, filled with various kinds of excellent food, drink, and edibles, one should visualize a wind mandala by means of the syllable *yaṃ*, and above that, a fire mandala by means of the syllable *raṃ*. Then...

Having visualized a lotus vessel resting upon a triple-stove (*muṇḍatraya*) constructed above three white *āḥ* syllables, one should produce therein the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*)—originating from the syllables *oṃ*, *trāṃ*, *āṃ*, *khaṃ*, *hūṃ*, *lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, *tāṃ*, and *vaṃ*—in the form of the five nectars and five lamps. Then, observing that the ten substances of the pledge (*samayadravya*), empowered by the ten seed-syllables, have been melted by the blazing fire impelled by the force of the wind-mandala, they take on the color of the newly risen sun.
[Thereupon,] a [light] standing at a distance of one span (*vitasti*) arises, generated from the mercury-colored syllable *hūṃ*.
One should visualize the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) as consisting of the nectar from the downward-facing [skull].
Then, one should contemplate that too as melting away with steam, merging together, becoming like mercury, and turning cool.

Upon that, having seen the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* transformed from the *āli* and *kāli*, one should contemplate that their rays of light draw in the wisdom-nectar (*jñānāmṛta*) of the heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*) residing in the ten directions, which then enter into those very syllables.

Then, having observed even the syllable *oṃ* and the others gradually dissolved, one should abide as desired by means of the three syllables alone. Then, having formed the *jvālāmudrā* and having summoned the Blessed Lady with the recitation of the syllable *pheṃ*, one should establish her before oneself, worship her preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*argha-pādya*) and so forth, and [place] both hands in the upward-opened *vajrāñjali*.

Having placed that vessel down and meditated, one should recite this for the purpose of accepting the *bali* offering: "The goddesses are the authority, the *samaya* is the authority, and their spoken words are the supreme authority.
By this truth, may these goddesses become the cause of my grace."

Then, one should rotate that vessel of nectar counter-clockwise while reciting three times: "Oṃ vajrāralli hoḥ hūṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ, you are the pledge (*samaya*) of Vajravārāhī, appear! Hoḥ! By means of this, one should offer it.
And the Blessed Lady [should partake] with the rays of light from her tongue, which is a white, single-pronged vajra arising from a subtle *hūṃ* syllable.
One should contemplate [the deity] as bringing delight to oneself.
Then, having offered betel-leaf and other items, worshipped, and praised [her], one should pray for the attainment of one's desired goal:
"Those whose attachment is equal to the cessation of existence, and whose attachment to worldly resolves has been shattered..."
Perceiving every state of being as if it were space, you whose ocean-like minds are overflowing with the waters of profound compassion— O Goddesses, bestow, bestow upon me your most intense pity!
Then, for those residing in the eight cremation grounds:

*Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali-offering! Protect the samaya! Grant me all siddhis! Eat, drink, and smell as you wish, according to your desire! Do not transgress! Be my companions for the increase of my own bliss in every way! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!*
*Phaṭ svāhā*. Having recited this three times, one should offer it.
By consuming that nectar, they should be visualized as flourishing.

Having offered betel leaves and other items collectively, having worshipped and praised [the deity], and having adorned [the mandala] with the *ācchomaka* hand-gesture, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra (*śatākṣara*) for the purpose of fulfilling any deficiencies or excesses in the ritual procedure.

Then, having satisfied [the deities] with the *kamalāvarta* mudrā, and while withdrawing that mudrā, one should perform the gesture of embracing; then, snapping the thumb and ring finger of the left hand while reciting "vajra mur," one should internalize that maṇḍala within oneself.
Thereafter, having made a formal prayer of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), one should move about in the form of the Goddess.
It is the traditional teaching that the bali offering should be given with the mantra of the Bhagavatī alone;
this procedure for the bali is indeed well-known.
Regarding the procedure for recitation (*japavidhi*):
since mantras accomplished with a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) prepared according to the prescribed rules grant excellent accomplishment, that method is briefly stated here.
"Akṣa" is said to be knowledge, which is the form of the deity as one has resolved upon it.
It is proclaimed in the tantras as the *akṣasūtra* because it indicates that [reality];
and it is called the *akṣasūtraka* because it indicates the syllables and the mantras.
Furthermore, the elision of the letter *r* is shown by its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group of words.
To destroy the entire web of afflictions, one who accomplishes the great purpose should, with those free from attachment, fashion a rosary that maintains happiness.
And it is said in the *Vikalparāja*: "In the case of the *niraṃśuka*, there is incantation for causing enmity.
And the *putrajīva* is declared to be effective for all rites when used in a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosed) form:
with one hundred [recitations] it is known as pacifying (*śāntika*), and with one hundred and eight, it is nourishing (*pauṣṭika*).
With twenty-five [recitations] one shall gain control; with fifty, it is effective for all rites.
Meru is proclaimed to be the embodiment of the true Dharma, such as the grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya) and so forth.
But for the purification of the *dharmadhātu*, some [use] other fingers above that;
thus, with nine threads spun by a maiden, they form the strands.
Emerging from the mouth and entering the lotus by way of the central channel, [the breath] passes again and again from the mouth into the lotus; such is the characteristic of the recitation (*jāpa*).
"A certain teacher of mine said that [the mantra] should emerge from the seed-syllable *vaṃ* alone;
since there is no purpose for it here, the other rosary has not been mentioned."
In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), one should employ the wrathful [deities]; in rites for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), from the central reality;
for subjugation (*vaśya*), it is said to be the ring finger; and for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), at the very end.
Thus ends the rule for the fingers in the *Vajraḍāka-kārikā*.
Thus ends the procedure for recitation (*japa*).
Regarding the procedure for maintaining the *samaya*: since accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs swiftly only for those who observe the *samaya*, some *samayas* are stated here.
And so it is said in the *Sādhana* of Śabara-pāda:
Better is the abandonment of life, better is the encounter with death,
if one who desires supreme accomplishment would always protect the samaya.
One should not abandon a mind of compassion even toward slanderers.
One must not perform malevolent magic against those of virtuous conduct who have committed offenses.
One should avoid the ostentatious display of one's own virtues for the sake of gain, honor, and the like.
Fear, pride, anger, greed, delusion, and so forth must be restrained;
one should always maintain the conduct of the Left (vāmācāra).
No distinction should be made between the mantra and the deity.

Having resolved upon the natural purity [of all things] and guarding against public censure, one should avoid deliberating over what is fit or unfit to be eaten. One should not excessively weary oneself with difficult austerities. Women should not be despised, especially those who bear the *mudrās*.
One should avoid sloth, torpor, restlessness, and so forth;
one should also avoid the eight root downfalls. One should always be skillful in the affairs of sentient beings.
Service such as bathing and so forth should be performed with diligence;
in this very manner, one should employ others in one's own work,
being entirely free from all suspicion and devoid of all dualities.
The yogin should conduct himself like a lion.
These and other commitments (samayas) taught therein must be observed;
furthermore, the commitments taught in the *Śabarapādīya-sādhana* should also be contemplated.
Thus concludes the procedure for maintaining the commitments (*samaya*).
This *Pañjikā* on the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi*, titled *Marmakalikā*, composed by the Great Paṇḍita Bhikṣu Vīryaśrīmitra of the illustrious Vikramaśīla Mahāvihāra, is completed.
By this merit that has been earned by writing this commentary on reality, may [all beings] attain the state of Buddhahood.
By this, may the entire world become a vessel for the perfect attainment of knowledge.
This king of books was transcribed by the student Vijayarakṣita in five days;
this manuscript was completed on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, in the year [indicated by] the moon, a dot, and the region, while Mars was in the sign of the Earth.
Then, during the conjunction of Āṣāḍha-pūrva-vārī-yāna, it was heard by the illustrious Raṇameghapālas.
This *Pañjikā* on the essence of the *Śrīmarmakalikā*, which is the knowledge of reality,
was heard by the wise Meghapāla, the sovereign over the five [kings].
